name: section-comment
summary: Comments used as dividers or section headers
explanation:
Flags own-line comments used as dividers or section headers. Such a comment groups code by its position in the file, and
nothing keeps that grouping accurate as code moves.

## Why is this bad?

A section comment groups code by its position in the file, and nothing keeps the grouping accurate as code moves. A
named function, class or module groups the same code under a name that tools can check.

## Example

```python report
# ---------- parsing ----------
def parse_header(line: str) -> str:
    return line.split(":", 1)[0]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def parse_header(line: str) -> str:
    return line.split(":", 1)[0]
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Divider lines**: comments made only of divider characters (`-`, `=`, `*`, `#`, `~`, `_`, `+`, `/`), at least four of
  them counting the leading `#`, such as `# ---` or `####`; they carry no text, only a visual break.

  ```python report
  # ----
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Decorated titles**: comments whose words are framed by divider characters, so the decoration frames them as a
  heading:

  - Three or more of the same divider character at the start or end, such as `# --- helpers`:

    ```python report
    # --- helpers
    def helper() -> None:
        pass
    ```

  - Two or more at both ends, each set apart from the words by a space, such as `# -- helpers --`:

    ```python report
    # -- helpers --
    def other() -> None:
        pass
    ```

- **Markdown-style headings**: comments that open with two or more `#`, such as `## Setup`, the way a document heading
  does.

  ```python report
  ## Setup
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Editor regions**: `# region` and `# endregion` markers, which fold code into named sections.

  ```python report
  # region parsing
  VALUE = 1
  # endregion
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Trailing comments**: a comment after code annotates its own line and cannot head a section.

  ```python ok
  VALUE = 1  # ---------- parsing ----------
  ```

- **Comments starting with `#!`**: this is a shebang line.

  ```python ok
  #!/usr/bin/env python3
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **[PEP 723](https://peps.python.org/pep-0723/) metadata**: the `# ///` lines open and close inline script metadata,
  which tools need in that exact form.

  ```python ok
  # /// script
  # requires-python = ">=3.12"
  # ///
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Prose that uses divider characters**: such as `# C++` or `# >>> run()`, they are words, not dividers.

  A run at one end counts only at three or more characters, since two also end words like `C++`. A pair needs a space
  between it and the words, so `# __init__ runs first, before __call__` passes.

  ```python ok
  # C++ is compiled ahead of time
  # >>> run()
  # __init__ runs first, before __call__
  VALUE = 1
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe, since comments do not affect behavior. What it does depends on the text left once the decoration is
gone:

- **Decoration only, or a title of up to three words**, as in `# === helpers ===`: the fix deletes the comment.

  ```python report
  # === helpers ===
  VALUE = 1
  ```

  ```python fixed
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Longer text**, such as an instruction: the fix strips the decoration and keeps a plain comment, so
  `#  *** remove return to update cron` becomes `# remove return to update cron`.

  ```python report
  #  *** remove return to update cron
  VALUE = 1
  ```

  ```python fixed
  # remove return to update cron
  VALUE = 1
  ```

A divider run joined to a word without a space, such as the `++` of `C++`, stays unless it is three characters or
longer.

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's
[multiple-leading-hashes-for-block-comment](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/multiple-leading-hashes-for-block-comment/)
also reports the `## Setup` form.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet. Preview rules
  [E265](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/no-space-after-block-comment/) and
  [E266](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/multiple-leading-hashes-for-block-comment/) reformat some of the same
  comments, such as `## Setup` or `#---`, but keep them.

def parse_header(line: str) -> str:
    return line.split(":", 1)[0]

# ----
VALUE = 1

## Setup
VALUE = 1

# region parsing
VALUE = 1
# endregion

#!/usr/bin/env python3
VALUE = 1

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# ///
VALUE = 1

# C++ is compiled ahead of time
# >>> run()
# __init__ runs first, before __call__
VALUE = 1

# === helpers ===
VALUE = 1
VALUE = 1

#  *** remove return to update cron
VALUE = 1

# remove return to update cron
VALUE = 1

name: long-paragraph
summary: Comment paragraphs over the word limit
explanation:
Flags comment paragraphs longer than 100 words by default, since a paragraph that long usually mixes topics and gets
skimmed.

## Why is this bad?

A paragraph that long usually covers more than one topic, and readers skim it. Split at a change of topic, each part is
easier to find and to keep accurate.

## Example

```python report
# Manifests are cached by path and modification time, because parsing them dominates the start-up time of large
# projects. An entry written by one interpreter is not valid for another, since the parsed form depends on the version
# of the grammar, so the cache directory is named after the interpreter. Entries older than thirty days are removed on
# the next run, and a corrupt entry is discarded rather than reported, because the file it came from is still on disk.
# Writes go to a temporary file first, then replace the entry, so a crash never leaves half of one behind. Readers
# never lock, since a replaced file is either the old one or the new one.
CACHE = {}
```

Use instead:

```python ok
# Manifests are cached by path and modification time, because parsing them dominates the start-up time of large
# projects. An entry written by one interpreter is not valid for another, so the cache directory is named after it.
#
# Entries older than thirty days are removed on the next run, and a corrupt entry is discarded rather than reported,
# because the file it came from is still on disk. Writes go to a temporary file first, then replace the entry, so a
# crash never leaves half of one behind.
CACHE = {}
```

## Configuration

- [`max-paragraph-words`](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/rule-settings.html#max-paragraph-words)
  in `[tool.simplint]`: the most words a paragraph may hold, 100 by default

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint]
  max-paragraph-words = 10
  ```

  ```python report
  # The cache keeps one entry per manifest, keyed by path and modification time.
  VALUE = 1
  ```

## What it does

No fix is offered, since where to split a paragraph depends on its meaning.

### Active on

- **Own-line comment paragraphs**: a **paragraph** is a run of own-line comments on consecutive lines at the same
  indentation, and it is reported once it passes `max-paragraph-words` words. Any of these ends it:

  - an empty `#` line
  - a line of code
  - a comment at another indentation

  ```python report
  # The cache keeps one entry per manifest, keyed by path and modification time, because parsing a manifest dominates
  # the start-up time of large projects. An entry written by one interpreter is not valid for another, since the parsed
  # form depends on the version of the grammar, so the cache directory is named after the interpreter. Entries older
  # than thirty days are removed on the next run, and a corrupt entry is discarded rather than reported, because the
  # file it came from is still on disk and can be parsed again. Writes go to a temporary file first, then replace the
  # entry, so a crash never leaves half of one behind. Readers never lock, since a replaced file is either the old one
  # or the new one.
  VALUE = 1
  ```

  ```python ok
  # The cache keeps one entry per manifest, keyed by path and modification time, because parsing a manifest dominates
  # the start-up time of large projects. An entry written by one interpreter is not valid for another, since the parsed
  # form depends on the version of the grammar, so the cache directory is named after the interpreter.
  #
  # Entries older than thirty days are removed on the next run, and a corrupt entry is discarded rather than reported,
  # because the file it came from is still on disk and can be parsed again. Writes go to a temporary file first, then
  # replace the entry, so a crash never leaves half of one behind. Readers never lock, since a replaced file is either
  # the old one or the new one.
  VALUE = 1
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Trailing comments**: a comment after code annotates that line, so it is not part of a paragraph.

  ```python ok
  VALUE = 1  # The cache keeps one entry per manifest, keyed by path and modification time, because parsing a manifest dominates the start-up time of large projects. An entry written by one interpreter is not valid for another, since the parsed form depends on the version of the grammar, so the cache directory is named after the interpreter. Entries older than thirty days are removed on the next run, and a corrupt entry is discarded rather than reported, because the file it came from is still on disk and can be parsed again. Writes go to a temporary file first, then replace the entry, so a crash never leaves half of one behind. Readers never lock, since a replaced file is either the old one or the new one.
  ```

### Report range

The report spans from the paragraph's first line to the line where it passes `max-paragraph-words` words.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rule
  [W505](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/doc-line-too-long/), which limits characters per line rather than words per
  paragraph; merged pull request [#1804](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/1804).

name: suppression-without-reason
summary: `noqa`, `type: ignore` and `pragma` comments with no reason
explanation:
Flags suppression comments, such as `# noqa: F401` or `# type: ignore[...]`, that give no reason.

## Why is this bad?

A suppression outlives the problem it hid. Without a reason, a later reader cannot tell whether the error is a false
positive, a known stub gap or a bug someone meant to fix, so nobody dares remove it.

## Example

```python report
import os  # noqa: F401

VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import os  # noqa: F401  # re-exported for plugins

VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]  # stub omits sep on this platform
```

## What it does

No fix is offered: only the author knows why the error was suppressed.

### Active on

Each of these suppression comments is reported when it has no **reason**: any text after the error codes, or another `#`
comment on the same line, or a comment on the line above. A comment with neither codes nor a reason is reported here for
the missing reason, and by [blanket-ignore](SMP004.html) for the missing codes.

- **Ruff**: [error suppression](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/#error-suppression) comments, in these forms:

  - `noqa`: a trailing comment with error codes. A code looks like
    [unused-import](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-import/): uppercase letters followed by digits.

    ```python report
    import os  # noqa: F401
    ```

  - `ruff: noqa`: the same suppression with the `ruff:` prefix, on a line of its own.

    ```python report
    # ruff: noqa: F401
    import os
    ```

  - `ruff: ignore[...]`: a trailing comment with codes in brackets.

    ```python report
    import sys  # ruff: ignore[unused-import]
    ```

  - `ruff: file-ignore[...]`: a comment on a line of its own with codes in brackets.

    ```python report
    # ruff: file-ignore[unused-import]
    import sys
    ```

- **simplint**: its own `simplint: ignore[...]`.

  ```python report
  VALUE = 1  # simplint: ignore[SMP101]
  ```

- **Type checkers**: [`type: ignore`](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/directives.html#type-ignore-comments),
  [`ty: ignore`](https://docs.astral.sh/ty/suppression/),
  [`pyright: ignore`](https://microsoft.github.io/pyright/#/comments), and
  [`pyrefly: ignore`](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/error-suppressions/). The `ignore` comments take their codes in
  brackets, with or without a space after the colon.

  ```python report
  VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
  OTHER = 1  # ty: ignore[unresolved-import]
  THIRD = 2  # pyright: ignore[reportGeneralTypeIssues]
  FOURTH = 3  # pyrefly: ignore[bad-assignment]
  ```

- **coverage.py**: [`pragma: no cover`](https://coverage.readthedocs.io/en/latest/excluding.html) and
  [`pragma: no branch`](https://coverage.readthedocs.io/en/latest/branch.html).

  ```python report
  if DEBUG:  # pragma: no cover
      VALUE = 1
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Suppressions with a reason**: any text after the codes, or another comment on the same line, counts as the reason.

  ```python ok
  import os  # noqa: F401  # re-exported for plugins

  VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]  # stub omits sep on this platform
  ```

- **A reason on the line above**: a comment on the line directly above a trailing suppression counts, as do the comment
  lines in a run that ends there. The reason may take several lines, but a blank line or a line of code ends the run,
  and a suppression on a line of its own takes no reason from above.

  ```python ok
  # the plugin under test expects a str, so the wrong type is deliberate
  value = 123  # ty: ignore[invalid-argument-type]
  ```

- **Words that only start with a directive**: a directive must be a whole word, so one followed by a letter, digit, `-`
  or `_`, such as `# noqa-ish`, is ordinary text, not a suppression.

  ```python ok
  NOTE = 9  # noqa-ish wording is prose
  ```

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet. Closed issue
  [#10070](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/10070) (fixed by pull request
  [#21294](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/21294)) only lets `--add-noqa` write a reason; no Ruff rule reports a
  suppression without one.

import os  # noqa: F401  # re-exported for plugins

VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]  # stub omits sep on this platform
import os  # noqa: F401

# ruff: noqa: F401
import os
import sys  # ruff: ignore[unused-import]

# ruff: file-ignore[unused-import]
import sys
VALUE = 1  # simplint: ignore[SMP101]

VALUE = os.sep  # type: ignore[attr-defined]

name: blanket-ignore
summary: Suppression comments that name no error code
explanation:
Flags suppression comments that name no error code, except the forms Ruff's PGH003, PGH004 and RUF103 report while the
project's Ruff configuration selects them, such as a bare `# noqa`, `# type: ignore` or `# ruff: ignore`. It covers the
rest, such as `# ty: ignore`. A blanket suppression hides every error on its line or in its file, including errors that
appear there later.

## Why is this bad?

A blanket suppression hides every error on its line, or in its file, including errors that appear there later. A real
bug that lands on the same line passes unnoticed, and the comment never says which error it was meant for.

## Example

```python report
VALUE = compute()  # ty: ignore
```

Use instead:

```python ok
VALUE = compute()  # ty: ignore[invalid-assignment]
```

## What it does

No fix is offered: the comment does not say which codes it should name.

### Active on

- **`noqa` after an earlier one**: Ruff reads only the first `noqa` of a comment, and a `noqa` it rejects still counts
  as that first one. A later bare `noqa` is therefore not reported by PGH004, and it is reported here.

  ```python report
  import os  # noqa: F401 # noqa
  ```

- **File-level `noqa` after an earlier one**: the same holds for `ruff: noqa` and `flake8: noqa` on a line of its own,
  where Ruff reads only the first one of a comment.

  ```python report
  # flake8: noqa # ruff: noqa
  import os
  ```

- **`ruff: ignore`, `ruff: file-ignore` and `simplint: ignore` without codes**: each directive whose brackets are
  missing or empty.

  ```python report
  VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore
  OTHER = 2  # simplint: ignore
  ```

  ```python report
  # ruff: file-ignore
  import os
  ```

- **`ty: ignore`, `pyrefly: ignore` without codes**: each directive whose brackets are missing or empty, with or without
  a reason after it, since the reason does not limit what it hides.

  ```python report
  VALUE = 1  # ty: ignore
  THIRD = 3  # pyrefly: ignore
  FIFTH = 5  # ty: ignore because the stub is wrong
  ```

- **`pyright: ignore` and `type: ignore` with a reason or empty brackets**: PGH003 reports these only when nothing
  follows `ignore` but whitespace or another comment. A reason after them, or empty brackets, leaves them to this rule.

  ```python report
  OTHER = 2  # pyright: ignore because the stub is wrong
  SIXTH = 6  # type: ignore because the stub is wrong
  FOURTH = 4  # type: ignore[]
  ```

- **Each directive of a comment**: a comment can hold several directives, and each one without codes is reported.

  ```python report
  TENTH = 10  # ty: ignore[unresolved-import] # pyrefly: ignore
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Directives that name codes**: `ty: ignore[code]` and `pyright: ignore[code]` limit the suppression to those errors,
  and `noqa: CODE` does the same for Ruff.

  ```python ok
  import os  # noqa: F401

  SEVENTH = 7  # ty:ignore[unresolved-import]
  EIGHTH = 8  # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]
  ```

- **Forms Ruff reports**: Ruff's PGH004 reports a bare `noqa`, a file-level `ruff: noqa` or `flake8: noqa`, and PGH003
  reports a bare `type: ignore` or `pyright: ignore`. This rule leaves them to Ruff only when the project's Ruff
  configuration selects that rule, and Ruff's own suppressions of it, through `per-file-ignores` or `noqa`, are
  respected too.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff.lint]
  select = ["PGH003", "PGH004"]
  ```

  ```python ok
  import os  # noqa

  # flake8: noqa
  VALUE = 1  # type: ignore
  ```

- **`ruff: ignore` and `ruff: file-ignore` without codes**: Ruff's
  [invalid-suppression-comment](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/invalid-suppression-comment/) (RUF103) reports them
  while the project's Ruff configuration selects it, and this rule leaves them to Ruff then.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff.lint]
  select = ["RUF103"]
  ```

  ```python ok
  VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore
  # ruff: file-ignore
  import os
  ```

- **`ruff: ignore` with a space before its codes**: Ruff reads the codes of `ruff: ignore [E501]` and
  `ruff: file-ignore [E501]`, so the directive is not a blanket one.

  ```python ok
  VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore [E501]
  ```

- **`noqa` comments Ruff rejects**: Ruff warns about a `noqa` whose colon names no code, or whose code runs into other
  text, and applies none of it, so the comment hides nothing.

  ```python ok
  import sys  # noqa: because plugins import it
  ```

- **File-level directives out of place**: Ruff applies `# ruff: noqa` only on a line of its own and
  `# ruff: file-ignore` only at module scope; anywhere else it warns and applies none of it.

  ```python ok
  import os  # ruff: noqa
  ```

- **Directives that take no codes**: coverage.py's pragmas name no error, so they are not blanket suppressions.

  ```python ok
  if DEBUG:  # pragma: no cover
      VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Words that only start with a directive**: a directive must be a whole word, so `ignored` after `ty: ignore` is
  ordinary text.

  ```python ok
  ELEVENTH = 11  # ty: ignored later
  ```

- **Text inside strings**: only comments count, so a directive written in a string literal is not checked.

  ```python ok
  THIRTEENTH = "# ty: ignore"
  ```

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's [blanket-noqa](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-noqa/) (PGH004) and
[blanket-type-ignore](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-type-ignore/) (PGH003) own the forms that name no code
and that Ruff reads as blanket: the first `noqa` of a comment and the first file-level `ruff: noqa` or `flake8: noqa`,
and a `type: ignore` or `pyright: ignore` with nothing after `ignore`. Ruff's
[invalid-suppression-comment](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/invalid-suppression-comment/) (RUF103) owns a
`ruff: ignore` or `ruff: file-ignore` whose brackets name no code. This rule leaves those forms to Ruff only while the
project's Ruff configuration selects the rule that reports them, and Ruff's own suppressions of it, through
`per-file-ignores` or `noqa`, are respected too. It keeps the rest, including the `noqa` that follows an earlier one in
the same comment, and the `ty`, `pyrefly` and `simplint` forms.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rules
  [PGH003](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-type-ignore/),
  [PGH004](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-noqa/) and
  [RUF103](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/invalid-suppression-comment/), which report a bare `type: ignore`, the
  first `noqa` of a comment, and `ruff: ignore` without codes; this rule leaves those to them and covers the `ty`,
  `pyright`, `pyrefly` and `simplint` directives and the rest.

VALUE = compute()  # ty: ignore[invalid-assignment]
import os  # noqa: F401 # noqa

# flake8: noqa # ruff: noqa
import os

VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore
OTHER = 2  # simplint: ignore

# ruff: file-ignore
import os

VALUE = 1  # ty: ignore
THIRD = 3  # pyrefly: ignore
FIFTH = 5  # ty: ignore because the stub is wrong

OTHER = 2  # pyright: ignore because the stub is wrong
SIXTH = 6  # type: ignore because the stub is wrong
FOURTH = 4  # type: ignore[]
TENTH = 10  # ty: ignore[unresolved-import] # pyrefly: ignore

import os  # noqa: F401

SEVENTH = 7  # ty:ignore[unresolved-import]
EIGHTH = 8  # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]

import os  # noqa

# flake8: noqa
VALUE = 1  # type: ignore

VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore
# ruff: file-ignore
import os
VALUE = 1  # ruff: ignore [E501]
import sys  # noqa: because plugins import it
import os  # ruff: noqa

if DEBUG:  # pragma: no cover
    VALUE = 1
ELEVENTH = 11  # ty: ignored later
THIRTEENTH = "# ty: ignore"

name: restating-comment
summary: Comments that only repeat the code below
explanation:
Flags own-line comments whose every word is an identifier or keyword of the statement below, such as `# close file`
above `file.close()`. A statement across several lines counts in full.

## Why is this bad?

A comment that repeats the line under it tells the reader nothing new, and it goes stale without anyone noticing when
the code changes. Comments are for the reasons behind the code, which the code cannot show.

## Example

```python report
# close file
file.close()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
file.close()
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Own-line comments above code**: every word of the comment appears among the identifiers and keywords of the next
  line. Words compare without case, and a name matches only as a whole, so `# create user` does not restate
  `create_user()`, which the comment would have to spell out as `create` and `user` on their own.

  Consecutive own-line comments form one block, which is judged as a whole and removed whole.

  ```python report
  def run(result: int) -> int:
      # return result
      return result
  ```

  ```python report
  # Create user
  user.create()
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Comments with a word the code lacks**: the comment says something the code does not, so it stays.

  ```python ok
  # create the user for the request
  user = create_user()
  ```

- **Comments with a colon**: a colon marks a label or a directive, such as `# Note: ` or `# type: ignore`.

  ```python ok
  # Note: create user
  user = create_user()
  ```

- **Comments that quote syntax**: punctuation other than a sentence's, such as `*`, `[`, `(`, `=` or `>`, writes a piece
  of syntax or a condition, which says more than the names in it.

  ```python ok
  # *args
  args.extend(extra)
  ```

  ```python ok
  # depth > limit
  depth = limit + 10
  ```

- **Trailing comments**: a comment after code describes that line, not the line below.

  ```python ok
  user = create_user()  # create user
  ```

### Fix

The fix deletes the comment's line. It is safe, since a comment never changes behavior, and the words it had are all in
the code it leaves in place.

```python report
# close file
file.close()
```

```python fixed
file.close()
```

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet.
- [flake8-comments](https://github.com/orsinium-labs/flake8-comments) reports the same comments as
  [CM001](https://github.com/orsinium-labs/flake8-comments/blob/master/flake8_comments/_checker.py), such as
  `# create user` above `user.create()`. It only reports them, where this rule's fix deletes the comment.

# close file
file.close()
file.close()

# Create user
user.create()

# create the user for the request
user = create_user()

# Note: create user
user = create_user()

# *args
args.extend(extra)

# depth > limit
depth = limit + 10
user = create_user()  # create user

# close file
file.close()
file.close()

name: string-statement-comment
summary: Bare strings used as comments instead of `#` comments
explanation:
Flags triple-quoted string statements used as comments: strings that are neither the docstring of a module, class or
function nor an attribute docstring.

## Why is this bad?

Python evaluates a bare string and throws it away, so it documents nothing the way a docstring does, and no tool reads
it as a comment either. Pylint reports it as a pointless statement. A `#` comment says the same thing where a reader
looks for it.

## Example

```python report
import math

"""Area of the unit circle."""
AREA = math.pi
```

Use instead:

```python ok
import math

# Area of the unit circle.
AREA = math.pi
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Strings between statements**: a triple-quoted string that is not the first statement of its body, and does not
  follow an assignment, is a comment in disguise.

  ```python report
  def run() -> None:
      start()
      """Start the worker before waiting."""
      wait()
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Docstrings**: the first statement of a module, class or function body is its docstring.

  ```python ok
  def run() -> None:
      "Start the worker and wait for it."
      start()
  ```

- **Attribute docstrings**: a string right after an assignment documents the attribute it assigns, as Sphinx reads it.

  ```python ok
  class Config:
      timeout = 3
      "Seconds to wait for the server."
  ```

- **Single-quoted strings**: a short quoted string often marks a line on purpose, such as a statement a tracer or a test
  expects to run, while triple quotes mark a block of text.

  ```python ok
  def run() -> None:
      start()
      "continued"
      wait()
  ```

### Fix

The fix writes each line of the string as a `#` comment at the statement's indentation, so the code after it keeps its
line numbers. It is safe for the program: a string statement does nothing when it runs. The fix does not apply when:

- every statement of its body is a string, since the body would be left empty
- the string shares its line with other code or a trailing comment, or is an implicit concatenation of several strings
- the text holds a backslash, since the compiler reads escapes and may warn or fail on them
- the module has a `from __future__` import, which the compiler checks against the statements before it
- a line of the text would start a tool directive, such as `# fmt: off`, or start with `!`
- a comment line would run past the comment width, which [Ruff E501](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/line-too-long/)
  then reports

Tools that read the source text, such as `inspect.getsource`, see the comments where the string was.

```python report
def run() -> None:
    start()
    """Start the worker.
    Then wait for it."""
    wait()
```

```python fixed
def run() -> None:
    start()
    # Start the worker.
    # Then wait for it.
    wait()
```

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's useless-expression rule (`B018`) skips string literals, so Ruff does not report these statements.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** open issue [#11292](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11292).
  Closed pull requests [#11302](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/11302) and
  [#27253](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/pull/27253) without a rule.
- [pylint](https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint) reports string statements that have no effect as
  [pointless-string-statement](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/warning/pointless-string-statement.html),
  with no fix. Its message suggests disabling the check for strings used as documentation, where this rule's fix turns
  the string into `#` comments.

"""Area of the unit circle."""
AREA = math.pi

import math

# Area of the unit circle.
AREA = math.pi

def run() -> None:
    start()
    """Start the worker before waiting."""
    wait()

def run() -> None:
    start()
    "continued"
    wait()

def run() -> None:
    start()
    """Start the worker.
    Then wait for it."""
    wait()

def run() -> None:
    start()
    # Start the worker.
    # Then wait for it.
    wait()

name: numeric-ignore
summary: Numeric codes in simplint ignore comments
explanation:
Flags numeric codes in `# simplint: ignore[...]` comments and replaces them with rule names.

## Why is this bad?

The name says what the suppression covers without looking up a code. It also stays readable when the comment is reviewed
outside a diagnostic report.

## Example

```python report
def initialize(build_data: dict[str, Any]) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[SMP602] # required signature
    pass
```

```python fixed
def initialize(build_data: dict[str, Any]) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[imprecise-annotation] # required signature
    pass
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Known numeric simplint codes** in `simplint: ignore[...]`. The fix replaces only the codes and preserves the other
  names, spacing, and reason in the comment.

  ```python report
  def run(value: Any) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[SMP602, single-letter-name] # external signature
      pass
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Rule names** already use the preferred form. Unknown codes are left as written.

  ```python ok
  def run(value: Any) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[imprecise-annotation] # external signature
      pass
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe and changes only known numeric codes inside the brackets.

    pass

def initialize(build_data: dict[str, Any]) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[imprecise-annotation] # required signature
    pass

def run(value: Any) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[SMP602, single-letter-name] # external signature
    pass

def run(value: Any) -> None:  # simplint: ignore[imprecise-annotation] # external signature
    pass

name: unused-ignore
summary: Unused selectors in simplint ignore comments
explanation:
Reports selectors in `# simplint: ignore[...]` comments that no longer suppress a report under the active rule settings.
Enable it with `--extend-select SMP009` when checking for obsolete ignores.

## Why is this bad?

An obsolete ignore makes it harder to tell which exceptions still matter. It can also hide a new report if the same rule
starts applying to that line later.

## Example

```python report
value = 1  # simplint: ignore[single-letter-name]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
value = 1
```

## What it does

The rule tests removals one selector at a time, then offers one safe fix for the file. It re-lints each proposed edit
that might be unused and keeps the selector if removing it exposes any report, including one from a different rule. When
a comment has several selectors, the fix keeps those that still suppress reports. When its last selector is unused, the
directive and its reason are removed, and a comment after them on the same line stays:

```python report
value = 1  # simplint: ignore[single-letter-name]  # wire order
```

```python fixed
value = 1  # wire order
```

The rule checks the rules currently selected for the file. If you run a narrow `--select`, selectors for rules outside
that selection can appear unused. Use the project's normal settings when cleaning up ignores.

name: single-letter-name
summary: Single-letter names outside comprehensions and conventional type parameters
explanation:
Flags single-letter names outside comprehensions and conventional type parameter declarations.

## Why is this bad?

A single letter says nothing about what the name holds, so the reader has to find where it is bound to learn it.
Comprehensions are exempt because the iterable the names come from sits right next to them.

## Example

```python report
def scale(v: float, f: float) -> float:
    r = v * f
    return round(r, 2)
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def scale(value: float, factor: float) -> float:
    scaled = value * factor
    return round(scaled, 2)
```

## What it does

No fix is offered, since a meaningful name cannot be derived from the code.

### Active on

- **Functions and classes**: their names show up at every call site, far from the definition that explains them.

  ```python report
  def f() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

- **Parameters**: the body reads them away from the signature, and callers see the name in the signature and keyword
  arguments. This covers:

  - Parameters of a `def`, such as `v` in `def scale(v: float)`:

    ```python report
    def scale(v: float) -> float:
        return v * 2
    ```

  - Parameters of a [lambda](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#lambda), such as `v` in `lambda v: v`:

    ```python report
    callback = lambda v: v
    ```

- **Assignment and [walrus](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#assignment-expressions) targets**: the
  value is computed once, and every later use relies on the name alone to say what it is.

  - `=` assignments, such as `r = 3`:

    ```python report
    r = 3
    print(r)
    ```

  - `:=` walrus targets, such as `n` in `if (n := 3) > 2`:

    ```python report
    if (n := 3) > 2:
        print(n)
    ```

- **`with ... as`, `except ... as` and `import ... as` names**: the alias replaces the expression, exception or module
  name that said what the value is.

  - `with ... as` names, such as `f` in `with open("data.txt") as f`:

    ```python report
    with open("data.txt") as f:
        print(f.read())
    ```

  - `except ... as` names, such as `e` in `except ValueError as e`:

    ```python report
    try:
        run()
    except ValueError as e:
        print(e)
    ```

  - `import ... as` names, such as `o` in `import os as o`:

    ```python report
    import os as o
    ```

- **[`match`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#the-match-statement) captures**: the case body
  reads the captured value under that name.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  ```

  ```python report
  value = 1
  match value:
      case x:
          print(x)
  ```

- **Mapping rest captures**: `**rest` in a mapping pattern binds the remaining keys, and the case body reads them under
  that name.

  ```python report
  value = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
  match value:
      case {"a": 1, **r}:
          print(r)
  ```

- **`for` loop targets**, such as `i` in `for i in range(3)`: a loop body can run for many lines, far from the `for`
  line that says what the name holds.

  ```python report
  for i in range(3):
      print(i)
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Names inside a comprehension**: every name inside a list, set or dictionary
  [comprehension](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#list-comprehensions) or a
  [generator expression](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#generator-expressions), including a walrus
  target or lambda parameter, so `[x * 2 for x in values]` is fine. The whole expression keeps the iterable next to
  every use of the name.

  ```python ok
  values = [1, 2]
  doubled = [x * 2 for x in values]
  ```

- **`_`**: the conventional throwaway name, which says the value is unused.

  ```python ok
  for _ in range(3):
      pass
  ```

- **Uppercase type parameters**: names such as `T` and `P` are conventional in generic signatures. This includes
  parameters in [PEP 695 syntax](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#type-params) and assignments to
  `typing.TypeVar`, `typing.TypeVarTuple` or `typing.ParamSpec` when the string argument matches the assigned name.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  ```

  ```python ok
  from typing import TypeVar

  T = TypeVar("T")


  def first[U](items: list[U]) -> U:
      return items[0]
  ```

  A lowercase name, mismatched string or different function named `TypeVar` does not qualify.

- **Parameters of a method decorated with
  [`@override`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.override)**: the method must keep the parameter
  names of the method it replaces.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  ```

  ```python ok
  from typing import override


  class Base:
      def run(self, value: int) -> None:
          pass


  class Child(Base):
      @override
      def run(self, v: int) -> None:
          pass
  ```

- **`l`, `I` and `O`**: Ruff's [ambiguous-variable-name](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-variable-name/),
  [ambiguous-class-name](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-class-name/) and
  [ambiguous-function-name](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-function-name/) report these letters wherever
  this rule would, so this rule leaves them to Ruff while the project's Ruff configuration selects the rule for the kind
  of binding. Ruff's own suppressions of it, through `per-file-ignores` or `noqa`, are respected too.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff.lint]
  select = ["E741"]
  ```

  ```python ok
  l = 3
  ```

### Reporting

Each name is reported once per scope, at its first binding.

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's E741, E742 and E743 report `l`, `I` and `O` on variables, parameters, except names, classes and functions, with
no fix. This rule leaves those three letters to Ruff at those sites, and only while the project's Ruff configuration
selects the rule of each kind. Ruff's own suppressions of it, through `per-file-ignores` or `noqa`, are respected too.
It keeps every other single letter, and the `l`, `I` and `O` that Ruff does not check: import aliases, `match` captures
and lowercase type parameters.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rules
  [E741](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-variable-name/),
  [E742](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-class-name/) and
  [E743](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-function-name/), which report `l`, `I` and `O` and which this rule
  leaves to them; issue [#4866](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/4866) asking for all single letters was closed
  as not planned.
- [flake8-variables-names](https://github.com/best-doctor/flake8-variables-names) reports single-letter names as
  [VNE001](https://github.com/best-doctor/flake8-variables-names/blob/master/flake8_variables_names/checker.py), but
  allows `i`, `_` and `T` by default. This rule flags `for i` loop targets but allows `T` only when it declares a type
  parameter.
- [wemake-python-styleguide](https://github.com/wemake-services/wemake-python-styleguide) reports short names as
  [WPS111](https://wemake-python-styleguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/usage/violations/naming.html#wemake_python_styleguide.violations.naming.TooShortNameViolation),
  with a configurable minimum length. It also checks module and attribute names, which this rule does not list.

name: module-variable-case
summary: Module variables not `UPPER_CASE`
explanation:
Flags module-scope variables whose name is not `UPPER_CASE`, such as `limit` or `logger`. A leading underscore stays as
it is: [module-variable-prefix](SMP404.html) checks it.

## Why is this bad?

Upper case tells a reader the name is a module-level value rather than a local, as
[PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#constants) writes constants. A module that keeps the same case for all its
constants makes them easy to pick out at every use.

## Example

```python report
limit = 3
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

__all__ = ["logger"]
```

Use instead:

```python ok
LIMIT = 3
LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)

__all__ = ["LOGGER"]
```

## Configuration

- [`naming.keep-names`](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/rule-settings.html#naming) in
  `[tool.simplint]`: module-scope names the rule leaves as they are, such as `keep-names = ["urlpatterns"]` under
  `[tool.simplint.naming]`

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint.naming]
  keep-names = ["limit"]
  ```

  ```python ok
  limit = 3
  ```

- The Python version the code targets, taken from the first of these that applies; see
  [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version):

  1. [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version) in `[tool.ruff]`: for
     the files a pattern matches

     ```toml config
     [tool.ruff.per-file-target-version]
     "legacy/*.py" = "py37"
     ```

     ```python report file=legacy/old.py
     limit = 3
     ```

     ```python report file=new.py
     limit = 3
     ```

  1. [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) in `[tool.ruff]`: for every other file

     ```toml config
     [tool.ruff]
     target-version = "py38"
     ```

     ```python report
     limit = 3
     ```

  1. [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python):
     its lowest version, when Ruff sets neither

     ```toml config
     [project]
     name = "demo"
     requires-python = ">=3.8"
     ```

     ```python report
     limit = 3
     ```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Every module-scope variable**: whatever its visibility, its name should be `UPPER_CASE`. A leading underscore stays
  as it is, so `_timeout` becomes `_TIMEOUT`.

  ```python report
  limit = 3
  _timeout = 5
  ```

- **Names another module in the run imports**: only the case changes, and the leading underscore stays, since the
  importer already depends on the name.

  ```python report file=config.py
  limit = 3
  ```

  ```python context file=consumer.py
  from config import limit

  print(limit)
  ```

- **Names bound with `:=`**: a walrus at module scope binds a module variable like any assignment.

  ```python report
  if (total := 3) > 2:
      pass
  ```

simplint reads `__all__` from assignments, `+=`, `.extend([...])` and `.append("name")` with string literals.

### Exceptions

- **An `__all__` built any other way**: its contents depend on how the module runs, so the rule is skipped. This covers:

  - A call, such as `list(...)` or `.remove(...)`:

    ```python ok
    limit = 3
    __all__ = list(["limit"])
    ```

  - A binding inside a nested block, such as an `if`, `try` or function:

    ```python ok
    limit = 3

    if FLAG:
        __all__ = ["limit"]
    ```

- **Dunder names**: Python and its tools give these their meaning by their exact spelling.

  ```python ok
  __version__ = "1.0"
  ```

- **Class-like names**, such as the type alias `Alias = int`: they follow the `CapWords` convention of classes.

  ```python ok
  Alias = int
  ```

- **Type aliases from a `type` statement**: the statement binds a type, not a value, so the name follows the convention
  of classes, whatever its case.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  ```

  ```python ok
  type vector = list[float]
  ```

- **Names bound and read only inside one module-level `if`, `try` or `with` block**: a block such as a version check
  binds a name for its own use, and nothing outside the block reads it. A name that another file reads stays here.

  ```python ok
  import sys

  if sys.version_info < (3, 10):
      msg = "requires Python 3.10"
      raise RuntimeError(msg)
  ```

- **Annotations alone under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`**: the rules no longer report a declaration with no value under
  `if TYPE_CHECKING:`, which only types a name that a module's PEP 562 `__getattr__` serves at runtime. Renaming one
  breaks the type checker's view of `module.log`, while `__getattr__` keeps serving it at runtime. An assigned name in
  the same block is still checked.

  ```python ok
  import typing

  if typing.TYPE_CHECKING:
      log: typing.Callable[[str], None]
  else:

      def __getattr__(name: str) -> object: ...
  ```

- **Names also bound by an import, `def` or `class`**: this rule skips them. This covers:

  - An import, such as `from json import dumps`: the import keeps the spelling of what it imports.

    ```python ok
    from json import dumps

    dumps = dumps
    ```

  - A `def` or `class`, such as `def limit()`: [unexported-public-name](SMP403.html) applies the underscore convention
    to functions and classes.

    ```python ok
    def limit() -> int:
        return 3


    limit = limit()
    ```

- **Aliases of a function the module defines**: an alias reads as the function, so it keeps the function's name, as a
  class alias does. An alias of an imported name is not covered, as the rule cannot tell what an import binds.

  ```python ok
  def build_cli() -> str:
      return "cli"


  _build_cli = build_cli
  ```

- **Names bound only as `for`, `with`, `except` or `match` targets**: these hold whatever the statement produces, not a
  value the module defines.

  ```python ok
  for item in range(3):
      pass
  ```

- **`mixedCase` names Ruff reports**: [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope/)
  reports a `mixedCase` module name at its binding, unless its `ignore-names` lists the name. When the project's Ruff
  configuration selects N816, the name is left to Ruff, even if this rule could rename it.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff.lint]
  select = ["N816"]
  ```

  ```python ok file=_module.py
  myValue = 3
  print(myValue)
  ```

- **`TYPE_CHECKING`**: type checkers recognize the guard by that name whatever its value.

  ```python ok
  from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

  if TYPE_CHECKING:
      pass
  ```

The rule also skips names that a tool or framework looks up by their current spelling, since renaming them breaks the
lookup:

- **pytest's module variables**:
  [`pytestmark`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/example/markers.html#marking-whole-classes-or-modules),
  [`pytest_plugins`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/plugins.html#requiring-loading-plugins-in-a-test-module-or-conftest-file),
  [`collect_ignore` and `collect_ignore_glob`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/example/pythoncollection.html#customizing-test-collection).

  ```python ok file=tests/test_api.py
  import pytest

  pytestmark = pytest.mark.slow
  ```

- **Every name in a `conf.py`**: [Sphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/configuration.html) reads its
  settings by their lowercase names.

  ```python ok file=conf.py
  project = "demo"
  ```

- **`revision`, `down_revision`, `branch_labels` and `depends_on` in an
  [Alembic](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html#create-a-migration-script) revision file**: a module
  that binds `revision` and `down_revision` and defines an `upgrade` function. The names place the file in the migration
  graph.

  ```python ok file=migrations/versions/abc123.py
  revision = "abc123"
  down_revision = None
  branch_labels = None
  depends_on = None


  def upgrade() -> None:
      pass
  ```

- **[gunicorn settings](https://gunicorn.org/reference/settings/)**, such as `bind`, `workers` or `timeout`, in a
  gunicorn configuration file: gunicorn reads them by these exact names.

  A configuration file is one whose name contains `gunicorn`, such as `gunicorn.conf.py`, or a module that binds at
  least three settings, one of them `bind`, `workers` or `worker_class`. Any file can be one, so the second test tells
  it from a module that happens to define a `timeout`.

  ```python ok file=gunicorn.conf.py
  bind = "0.0.0.0:8000"
  workers = 4
  ```

- **`version`, `version_tuple` and `commit_id` in a module that also binds `__version__`**: the names of the version
  file [setuptools-scm](https://setuptools-scm.readthedocs.io/latest/usage/#version-files) writes.

  ```python ok
  __version__ = "1.0"
  version = "1.0"
  version_tuple = (1, 0, 0)
  commit_id = None
  ```

- **`apilevel`, `threadsafety` and `paramstyle` in a module that binds all three**: the
  [PEP 249](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/#globals) globals of a database driver.

  ```python ok
  apilevel = "2.0"
  threadsafety = 1
  paramstyle = "qmark"
  ```

- **PLY grammar names**: in a module that imports [PLY](https://github.com/dabeaz/ply)'s `lex` or `yacc`, including a
  vendored copy such as `pkg._ply.yacc`, the names `tokens`, `literals`, `precedence`, `states`, `start` and the `t_`
  and `p_` rules, which PLY reads off the module by name.

  ```python ok
  from ply import lex

  tokens = ("NUMBER",)
  ```

- **Every name in a PLY table module**, one that binds `_tabversion`: PLY reads its tables back by name.

  ```python ok
  _tabversion = "3.10"
  limit = 3
  ```

- **`app` and `application` bound to a WSGI, ASGI or [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/typer-command/)
  application**: servers and the `typer` command load the application by this name.

  The name must be assigned at the top level of the module from one of these calls: `aiohttp.web.Application`,
  `bottle.Bottle`, Django's `get_wsgi_application` and `get_asgi_application`, `falcon.App`, `falcon.API` and
  `falcon.asgi.App`, `fastapi.FastAPI`, `flask.Flask`, `litestar.Litestar`, `quart.Quart`, `sanic.Sanic`,
  `starlette.applications.Starlette`, `typer.Typer`, and Pyramid's `make_wsgi_app()`; the call is resolved through the
  module's imports.

  ```python ok
  from fastapi import FastAPI

  app = FastAPI()
  ```

- **The names listed in `naming.keep-names`**, under Configuration above: for any other framework that reads a module
  variable by name.

### Fix

The fix renames every use in the file, including the `__all__` entry, and keeps the leading underscore of the name.
**Unsafe fix:** always, as importers outside the run keep the old name, and so do string references in unchecked files,
such as [`mocker.patch`](https://pytest-mock.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage.html) targets. Code that loads a module
under a name no file of the run defines, such as a test that copies a file's text into a module and reads its names off
the copy, keeps the old name too.

```python report
limit = 3
print(limit)
```

```python fixed
LIMIT = 3
print(LIMIT)
```

A name read in an f-string field with a [`=`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#f-strings) debug
specifier keeps its printed text: the field prints the old name, then the value in a plain field.

```python report
limit = 3
print(f"{limit=}")
```

```python fixed
LIMIT = 3
print(f"limit={LIMIT!r}")
```

No fix is offered when:

- a public module of a library offers the name, as a public name or one `__all__` lists: its users import it, so the
  report stays and the author renames it by hand

- code the index cannot follow may read the name: a module the run cannot resolve binds it, such as a stdlib or
  third-party import, or a doctest spells it. The report stays, since such a read does not show what it reads

- another module in the run imports the name, reaches it by a dotted string, such as a `mocker.patch` target, or assigns
  it as an attribute of its module, as `module.NAME = value` or `setattr(module, "NAME", value)` does, since the rename
  would leave that write pointing at the old name

  ```python report file=config.py
  limit = 3
  ```

  ```python context file=consumer.py
  from config import limit

  print(limit)
  ```

- a file of the run reads an attribute by that name off a module it loads by a computed name: the result of
  `importlib.import_module`, `__import__` or `sys.modules[...]`, a parameter annotated `ModuleType`, or a pytest fixture
  that returns such a module

  ```python report file=loader.py
  limit = 3
  ```

  ```python context file=reader.py
  import importlib

  value = importlib.import_module("loader").limit
  ```

- a file of the run sets an attribute of the module under a computed name, as `setattr(module, name, value)` or
  `mock.patch(f"module.{name}")` does

- the new name is already used as a name in the file

  ```python report
  limit = 3
  LIMIT = 4
  print(limit, LIMIT)
  ```

- the name shadows a builtin, as in `zip = zip`, where the value reads the builtin under the same name

  ```python report
  zip = zip
  ```

- the old name appears in the text of a string of any file in the run, as written or through an escape such as
  `\N{LATIN SMALL LETTER X}`, other than an entry of an `__all__` list assigned with `=` or `+=`

  ```python report
  limit = 3
  NAME = "limit"
  ```

- the old name is read in a t-string, which keeps the source text of its expressions

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.14"
  ```

  ```python report
  limit = 3
  template = t"{limit}"
  print(template.interpolations[0].expression)
  ```

- the old name also names something a text rename cannot tell apart: a parameter, a local variable, a class attribute, a
  keyword argument or an attribute access

  ```python report
  limit = 3


  def scale(limit: int) -> int:
      return limit
  ```

### Related rules

[module-variable-prefix](SMP404.html) checks the leading underscore of the same variables.
[unexported-public-name](SMP403.html) applies the underscore convention to functions and classes.

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's [mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope/)
flags only `mixedCase` names. This rule flags `lower_case` names and leaves `mixedCase` names to Ruff whenever the
project's Ruff configuration selects N816. Ruff's own suppressions of it, through `per-file-ignores` or `noqa`, are
respected too.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rule
  [N816](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/mixed-case-variable-in-global-scope/), which reports only `mixedCase` names,
  without a fix; this rule leaves those names to Ruff and reports `lower_case` names, which it can rename to
  `UPPER_CASE`.
- [pylint](https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint) reports module-level assignments that do not match `const-naming-style`
  as [invalid-name](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/convention/invalid-name.html). It
  defaults to `UPPER_CASE` and only reports, where this rule renames the uses in the file.

name: meaningless-name
summary: Variables, parameters and attributes named with a word that says nothing
explanation:
Flags variables, parameters and attributes named with a placeholder word that says nothing about what they hold, such as
`foo` or `baz`. The words come from a list you can change.

## Why is this bad?

A name is the only description a value carries at each place it is used. `foo` leaves the reader to find where it is
assigned, and then to learn what it is. A name for the contents, such as `counts`, answers that at once.

## Example

```python report
def load(payload: bytes) -> dict[str, int]:
    foo = parse(payload)
    return foo
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def load(payload: bytes) -> dict[str, int]:
    counts = parse(payload)
    return counts
```

## Configuration

- [`naming.meaningless-names`](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/rule-settings.html#naming) in
  `[tool.simplint]`: the words to report, `foo`, `baz`, `qux` and `quux` by default. Words such as `data`, `result`,
  `value` or `tmp` are left out: a parser's `feed(data)`, a `for key, value in` loop or a `tmp` directory reads well in
  context. A list replaces the default one, so a project that bans more words lists the defaults too.

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint.naming]
  meaningless-names = ["foo", "baz", "tmp"]
  ```

  ```python report
  tmp = load()
  ```

## What it does

Reported names are the ones the list holds, compared as whole names, so `foo_count` is not `foo`. A word matches in
lower case, or in upper case as a constant spells it, with or without leading or trailing underscores.

### Active on

- **Variables**: names bound by assignment, `for` loops, `with ... as` and the walrus operator.

  ```python report
  foo = 3
  ```

  ```python report
  _FOO = 3
  ```

  ```python report
  for foo in items:
      print(foo)
  ```

- **Parameters** of a function or a lambda.

  ```python report
  def scale(factor: float, foo: float) -> float:
      return factor * foo
  ```

- **Exception and `match` names**: the name `except ... as` and a `case` capture binds.

  ```python report
  try:
      run()
  except OSError as foo:
      print(foo)
  ```

- **Attributes a method declares**: `self.name = ...` in a method, or `cls.name = ...` in a classmethod.

  ```python report
  class Cache:
      def __init__(self) -> None:
          self.foo = {}
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Overrides**: the parameters of a method decorated with
  [`@override`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.override) keep the names of the method they
  replace.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  requires-python = ">=3.12"
  ```

  ```python ok
  from json import JSONEncoder
  from typing import override


  class Encoder(JSONEncoder):
      @override
      def default(self, foo: object) -> object:
          return str(foo)
  ```

- **Dunder methods**: the parameters of a method named with double underscores, such as `value` in `__setitem__`, keep
  the names of the protocol they implement.

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint.naming]
  meaningless-names = ["value"]
  ```

  ```python ok
  class Store:
      def __setitem__(self, key: str, value: int) -> None:
          self.items = {key: value}
  ```

- **Attributes written through other objects**: `response.foo = ...` names an attribute the code does not choose.

  ```python ok
  def fill(response) -> None:
      response.foo = b""
  ```

- **Names outside the list**: a name that merely contains a listed word is a name with a meaning.

  ```python ok
  foo_count = load()
  ```

- **Class names**: `Foo` names a class, which the rule does not check where it is defined, so a `Foo = ...` that rebinds
  one is not reported either.

  ```python ok
  Foo = make_class()
  ```

### Reporting

Each name is reported once per scope, at its first binding, as [single-letter-name](SMP101.html) reports its names.

## Ruff overlap

Ruff's [ambiguous-variable-name](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ambiguous-variable-name/) covers `l`, `O` and `I`
only. This rule covers a word list you choose, like pylint's
[disallowed-name](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/convention/disallowed-name.html).

## Fix

No fix is offered, since a meaningful name cannot be derived from the code.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** open issues [#970](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/970),
  [#3845](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/3845) and [#3463](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/3463).
- [flake8-variables-names](https://github.com/best-doctor/flake8-variables-names) reports placeholder names such as
  `data` as
  [VNE002](https://github.com/best-doctor/flake8-variables-names/blob/master/flake8_variables_names/checker.py). Its
  strict option adds more words.
- [wemake-python-styleguide](https://github.com/wemake-services/wemake-python-styleguide) reports a fixed list of
  blacklisted names as
  [WPS110](https://wemake-python-styleguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/usage/violations/naming.html#wemake_python_styleguide.violations.naming.WrongVariableNameViolation).
- [pylint](https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint) reports the names in its
  [disallowed-name](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/convention/disallowed-name.html) list.
  That list defaults to placeholders such as `foo` and `bar`, not words such as `data`.

name: catch-all-module
summary: Modules and packages named for a grab bag of code
explanation:
Flags modules and packages named for a grab bag of code, such as `utils`, `helpers` or `common`. The names come from a
list you can change.

## Why is this bad?

A module named `utils` collects whatever did not fit elsewhere, and its name says nothing about any of it. Imports from
it read the same whatever they bring in, and the module keeps growing.

## Example

```python report file=utils.py
def slugify(text: str) -> str:
    return text.lower().replace(" ", "-")
```

Use instead:

```python ok file=slugs.py
def slugify(text: str) -> str:
    return text.lower().replace(" ", "-")
```

## Configuration

- [`naming.catch-all-modules`](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/rule-settings.html#naming) in
  `[tool.simplint]`: the module and package names to report. A list replaces the default one, which holds `utils`,
  `util`, `utilities`, `helpers`, `helper`, `common` and `misc`.

  ```toml config
  [tool.simplint.naming]
  catch-all-modules = ["utils", "helpers", "misc"]
  ```

  ```python report file=helpers.py
  def parse() -> None:
      pass
  ```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Modules**: a file named for an entry of the list, such as `utils.py`.

  ```python report file=common.py
  VALUE = 1
  ```

- **Packages**: an `__init__.py` in a folder named for an entry of the list, such as `utils/__init__.py`.

  ```python report file=utils/__init__.py
  VALUE = 1
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Modules in a catch-all package**: `utils/slugs.py` keeps its own name, and the package is reported through its
  `__init__.py`. A folder without an `__init__.py` is not reported.

  ```python ok file=utils/slugs.py
  def slugify(text: str) -> str:
      return text.lower().replace(" ", "-")
  ```

- **Names outside the list**: `models.py` is the name Django reads for a project's models, and `types.py` or
  `interfaces.py` usually holds one kind of code, type aliases or protocols, so the default list leaves them out. A
  project whose `types` is a grab bag adds it to `catch-all-modules`.

  ```python ok file=models.py
  VALUE = 1
  ```

  ```python ok file=types.py
  Slug = str
  ```

## Fix

No fix is offered. A rename changes every import of the module, and a split needs to know what each part holds.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** open issue [#3845](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/3845).
- [wemake-python-styleguide](https://github.com/wemake-services/wemake-python-styleguide) reports modules named for a
  blacklisted word, such as `utils`, as
  [WPS100](https://wemake-python-styleguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/usage/violations/naming.html#wemake_python_styleguide.violations.naming.WrongModuleNameViolation).

name: entrypoint-module-name
summary: Entrypoints in `main.py` or `_main.py` instead of `__main__.py`
explanation:
Flags `main.py` and `_main.py` when they serve as command entrypoints.

## Why is this bad?

Python looks for a package's [`__main__.py`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html#main-py-in-python-packages)
when it runs `python -m package`. Keeping the command's entrypoint there makes the executable module easy to find and
lets the same package run through `-m`. A separate `_main.py` can still hold the implementation when `__main__.py`
imports and calls it.

## Example

```toml config
[project]
name = "pkg"
version = "1"

[project.scripts]
pkg = "pkg.main:run"
```

```python context file=pkg/__init__.py
"""The package."""
```

```python report file=pkg/main.py
def run() -> None:
    print("ready")
```

Use instead:

```toml config
[project]
name = "pkg"
version = "1"

[project.scripts]
pkg = "pkg.__main__:run"
```

```python ok file=pkg/__main__.py
def run() -> None:
    print("ready")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
```

## What it does

The rule reports a file named `main.py` or `_main.py` when a `[project.scripts]` or `[project.gui-scripts]` entry in
`pyproject.toml` names its module, or when the file has a top-level `if __name__ == "__main__":` block. It does not
report the filename alone.

### Exceptions

- **Implementation modules:** `_main.py` can hold a command's implementation when the configured entrypoint names
  `__main__.py` instead.
- **Other entry points:** plugin objects in `[project.entry-points]` do not make their module a command entrypoint.

## Fix

No fix is offered. Renaming an entrypoint also requires updating its imports and script declaration.
