name: all-not-last
summary: `__all__` not at the end of the module
explanation:
Flags modules where the last top-level statement that binds `__all__` is not the last statement. At the end of the
module the export list comes after every definition it names, so it reads as a summary of what the module provides.

## Why is this bad?

Readers look for the export list in one place. At the end of the module it comes after every definition it names, so it
reads as a summary of what the module provides. [missing-from-all](SMP401.html) and [all-format](SMP405.html) also check
`__all__`.

## Example

```python report
__all__ = ["main"]


def main() -> None:
    run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Use instead:

```python ok
def main() -> None:
    run()


__all__ = ["main"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Bindings of [`__all__`](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/modules.html#importing-from-a-package) followed by other
  statements**: the last top-level statement that binds `__all__` is reported when a statement comes after it, other
  than a call on `__all__` (see Exceptions). An assignment, an annotated assignment or an augmented assignment binds it.

  - an assignment, followed by a call:

    ```python report
    __all__ = ["main"]


    def main() -> None:
        pass


    main()
    ```

  - an annotated assignment, followed by a call:

    ```python report
    __all__: list[str] = ["main"]


    def main() -> None:
        pass


    main()
    ```

  - an augmented assignment such as `+=`, followed by a `def`:

    ```python report
    __all__ = []
    __all__ += ["main"]


    def main() -> None:
        pass
    ```

  - a trailing `if` other than a `__main__` block, such as `if __name__ != "__main__":`, which counts as a regular
    statement:

    ```python report
    __all__ = ["main"]


    def main() -> None:
        pass


    if __name__ != "__main__":
        main()
    ```

### Exceptions

- **A trailing [`if __name__ == "__main__":`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html#idiomatic-usage) block**:
  it may follow `__all__`, since it runs the module as a script once everything above it is defined.

  - written as `if __name__ == "__main__":`:

    ```python ok
    def main() -> None:
        pass


    __all__ = ["main"]


    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()
    ```

  - with the operands swapped, as `if "__main__" == __name__:`:

    ```python ok
    def main() -> None:
        pass


    __all__ = ["main"]


    if "__main__" == __name__:
        main()
    ```

- **Calls on `__all__` after its binding**, such as `__all__.extend(...)` or `__all__.append(...)`: a call changes the
  list the binding made, so the calls stay with it. The binding and its calls form one block, which must still be last.

  ```python ok
  def main() -> None:
      pass


  __all__ = ["main"]
  __all__.extend(["stop"])
  __all__.append("halt")
  ```

  ```python report
  __all__ = ["main"]
  __all__.append("stop")


  def main() -> None:
      pass
  ```

### Fix

The fix is safe. It moves the statement to the end of the module, before a trailing `__main__` block, with two blank
lines before it, also when the file has no trailing newline. Comments further up stay where they are. A comment on the
line directly above the statement blocks the fix, and so does one above a `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` pair around the
statement; the pair itself moves with it.

```python report
__all__ = ["main"]


def main() -> None:
    run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python fixed
def main() -> None:
    run()


__all__ = ["main"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The fix is offered only when:

- a single statement binds `__all__`, to a list or tuple of string literals
- no later statement reads `__all__` or calls a method on it
- no later statement reads `__all__` at run time, through an attribute such as `sys.modules[__name__].__all__`, a
  `"__all__"` string or a call to `globals()`, `vars()` or `dir()`
- no function or lambda reads `__all__`, by name or at run time, wherever it is defined
- the statement shares no line with other code
- no comment sits on the line above it, or above the `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` pair around it

With several bindings or a later reader, moving the statement could change the value of `__all__` or what that reader
sees:

```python report
__all__ = ["main"]
__all__ += ["stop"]


def main() -> None:
    pass
```

```python fixed
__all__ = ["main"]
__all__ += ["stop"]


def main() -> None:
    pass
```

```python report
__all__ = ["main"]


def main() -> None:
    pass


print(__all__)
```

```python fixed
__all__ = ["main"]


def main() -> None:
    pass


print(__all__)
```

A module that reads `__all__` at run time still needs it bound above, so the statement is reported without a fix when
the module reads it through:

- an attribute, such as `sys.modules[__name__].__all__`:

  ```python report
  import sys

  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sys.modules[__name__].__all__)
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import sys

  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sys.modules[__name__].__all__)
  ```

- the string `"__all__"`, such as in `getattr(sys.modules[__name__], "__all__")`:

  ```python report
  import sys

  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(getattr(sys.modules[__name__], "__all__"))
  ```

  ```python fixed
  import sys

  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(getattr(sys.modules[__name__], "__all__"))
  ```

- a call to `globals()`:

  ```python report
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sorted(globals()))
  ```

  ```python fixed
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sorted(globals()))
  ```

- a call to `vars()`:

  ```python report
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sorted(vars()))
  ```

  ```python fixed
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(sorted(vars()))
  ```

- a call to `dir()`:

  ```python report
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(dir())
  ```

  ```python fixed
  __all__ = ["main"]


  def main() -> None:
      pass


  print(dir())
  ```

- a function or lambda that reads it when called, by name or with `globals()`, `vars()` or `dir()`, even one defined
  above the statement:

  ```python report
  def check() -> list[str]:
      return [globals()[name] for name in __all__]


  __all__ = ["check"]


  RESULT = check()
  ```

  ```python fixed
  def check() -> list[str]:
      return [globals()[name] for name in __all__]


  __all__ = ["check"]


  RESULT = check()
  ```

- a lambda that calls `dir()`, even one defined above the statement:

  ```python report
  read = lambda: sorted(dir())


  __all__ = ["check"]


  def check() -> list[str]:
      return read()
  ```

  ```python fixed
  read = lambda: sorted(dir())


  __all__ = ["check"]


  def check() -> list[str]:
      return read()
  ```

A value that depends on where it runs, such as a comprehension over `dir()`, gives another list once the statement
moves, so only a list or tuple of string literals is moved:

```python report
__all__ = [name for name in dir() if not name.startswith("_")]


def helper() -> str:
    return "helper"
```

```python fixed
__all__ = [name for name in dir() if not name.startswith("_")]


def helper() -> str:
    return "helper"
```

A comment on the line above the statement would stay behind on the line above the next statement, so the statement is
reported without a fix:

```python report
import os


# The public API of this module.
__all__ = ["helper"]


def helper() -> str:
    return os.sep
```

```python fixed
import os


# The public API of this module.
__all__ = ["helper"]


def helper() -> str:
    return os.sep
```

The same holds for a comment above a `# fmt: off` / `# fmt: on` pair around the statement, which would stay behind as
well:

```python report
import os


# The public API of this module.
# fmt: off
__all__ = ["helper"]
# fmt: on


def helper() -> str:
    return os.sep
```

```python fixed
import os


# The public API of this module.
# fmt: off
__all__ = ["helper"]
# fmt: on


def helper() -> str:
    return os.sep
```

A statement that shares its line with other code is reported without a fix as well:

```python report
# fmt: off
__all__ = ["main"]; VERSION = "1"
# fmt: on


def main() -> None:
    pass
```

```python fixed
# fmt: off
__all__ = ["main"]; VERSION = "1"
# fmt: on


def main() -> None:
    pass
```

### Related rules

[all-format](SMP405.html) checks the shape of `__all__` itself: a list, not a tuple, with a trailing comma.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet.

def helper() -> str:

import os

def main() -> None:

def main() -> None:

name: init-module-content
summary: `__init__.py` holding code beyond its API
explanation:
Flags `__init__.py` files that hold code beyond a module docstring and deliberate API re-exports. Importing any
submodule runs the package's `__init__.py` first, so code there can slow down or break unrelated modules.

## Why is this bad?

Python runs a package's `__init__.py` before it imports any of the package's submodules. Importing `pkg.sub` therefore
also runs everything in `pkg/__init__.py`, and a slow or failing import there slows down or breaks unrelated modules.
Unplanned re-exports give one object two import paths and invite circular imports. A package can deliberately expose
selected names from private modules through `__all__`.

## Example

```python context file=http_client/client.py
class Client:
    pass
```

```python report file=http_client/__init__.py
"""HTTP client."""

from .client import Client
```

Use instead:

```python context file=http_client/client.py
class Client:
    pass
```

```python ok file=http_client/__init__.py
"""HTTP client."""
```

Importers then use `from http_client.client import Client`. When the package presents an API, keep the implementation in
a private module and list the names it exposes:

```python context file=http_client/_client.py
class Client:
    pass
```

```python ok file=http_client/__init__.py
"""HTTP client."""

from ._client import Client

__all__ = ["Client"]
```

## What it does

No fix is offered: removing the code breaks every importer that relies on it, and moving it needs a decision about where
it belongs.

### Active on

- **Statements after the docstring of an
  [`__init__.py`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/import.html#regular-packages)** that do not form an explicit API:
  imports absent from [`__all__`](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/modules.html#importing-from-a-package) and direct
  definitions are reported.

  ```python report file=pkg/__init__.py
  """HTTP client."""

  from .client import Client
  ```

- **Other statements in a public package of a library**: anything beyond the re-exports listed under Exceptions is
  reported there too.

  - an import of a name it does not export:

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python report file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    from ._core import run
    from ._core import stop as stop

    __all__ = ["stop"]
    ```

  - any other statement, such as an assignment:

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python report file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    VERSION = "1.0"
    ```

### Exceptions

- **Test packages and nested test projects**: fixtures may need initializer code to exercise import behavior. A package
  under a test root that is itself a project is treated as test input, even when its module name does not start with
  `test_`.

- **PEP 562 package hooks and `if TYPE_CHECKING` blocks**: `__getattr__` can load package attributes on demand,
  `__dir__` can list them, and a `TYPE_CHECKING` block can expose their types to type checkers. The imports used by
  those hooks may still need a suppression when they are not re-exports.

- **The module docstring**: it documents the package and runs no code.

  ```python ok file=pkg/__init__.py
  """HTTP client."""
  ```

- **Names listed in `__all__`**: any package can expose selected names from a private module. The list must be readable
  statically; an unlisted import is still reported. This works in applications and private subpackages as well as public
  library packages.

  ```python context file=pkg/_api.py
  class API:
      pass
  ```

  ```python ok file=pkg/__init__.py
  from ._api import API

  __all__ = ["API"]
  ```

- **Other re-exports in a public package of a library**:
  [PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#public-and-internal-interfaces) describes a package's `__init__` exposing
  functionality from submodules. A public library package may also hold:

  - a redundant alias, such as `from ._core import run as run`:

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python ok file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    from ._core import run as run
    ```

  - `import *`:

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python ok file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    from ._core import *
    ```

  - `from __future__` imports, which change no behavior at run time

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python ok file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    from __future__ import annotations
    ```

  - `__lazy_modules__`, the modules Python 3.15 loads lazily when the package's imports run

    ```toml config
    [build-system]
    requires = ["setuptools"]
    build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

    [project]
    name = "demo"
    ```

    ```python ok file=demo/__init__.py
    """HTTP client."""

    __lazy_modules__ = ["demo._core"]

    from ._core import run

    __all__ = ["run"]
    ```

- **Statements Ruff reports**: with Ruff's preview mode on and
  [RUF067](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/non-empty-init-module/) selected, Ruff reports the statements of an
  `__init__.py` that it does not allow, so this rule leaves them to Ruff. Ruff allows imports, dunder assignments and
  `if TYPE_CHECKING` blocks, unless `strictly-empty-init-modules` is set.

  ```toml config
  [tool.ruff.lint]
  preview = true
  select = ["RUF067"]
  ```

  ```python ok file=pkg/__init__.py
  """HTTP client."""

  VERSION = "1.0"
  ```

### Public packages

A package is **public** when it belongs to one of the library's API packages and no part of its path starts with `_`;
see [undocumented-public-api](SMP903.html).

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of preview rule
  [RUF067](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/non-empty-init-module/), which reports code in `__init__.py` except imports
  and dunder assignments (all of it with `strictly-empty-init-modules`) and which this rule leaves to it; this rule also
  reports the imports a library's public package does not re-export.
- [wemake-python-styleguide](https://github.com/wemake-services/wemake-python-styleguide) reports logic in an `__init__`
  module as
  [WPS412](https://wemake-python-styleguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/usage/violations/best_practices.html#wemake_python_styleguide.violations.best_practices.InitModuleHasLogicViolation),
  with no fix.

name: test-only-code
summary: Module-level functions and classes only test modules use
explanation:
Flags module-level functions and classes that only test modules use, since they belong in the tests.

## Why is this bad?

Code that only tests call is test support, and it ships with the product. Readers take it for part of the package, and
it outlives the tests that needed it. Moving it into the tests, or into a test helper module, keeps the package to what
the program runs.

## Example

```python context file=tests/test_builders.py
from app.builders import build_fixture


def test_build() -> None:
    assert build_fixture() == {"id": 1}
```

```python report file=app/builders.py
def build_fixture() -> dict[str, int]:  # only tests call it
    return {"id": 1}
```

Use instead:

```python context file=tests/test_builders.py
from app.builders import build_fixture


def test_build() -> None:
    assert build_fixture() == {"id": 1}
```

```python ok file=tests/helpers.py
def build_fixture() -> dict[str, int]:
    return {"id": 1}
```

## What it does

### Active on

- **Module-level functions and classes** whose every reference in the run comes from a test module. A reference is an
  import, a call, an attribute read through the module, or a dotted string the index records. Methods are not covered
  yet, so a method used only by tests is not reported.

  ```python report file=app/builders.py
  def build_fixture() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_builders.py
  from app.builders import build_fixture


  def test_build() -> None:
      assert build_fixture() == 1
  ```

- **References through the module or a dotted string**: `module.name` in a test and a `"pkg.module.name"` string, such
  as the target of `mock.patch`, count as references to `name`.

  ```python report file=app/builders.py
  def build_fixture() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_builders.py
  from unittest import mock

  import app.builders as builders


  def test_build() -> None:
      assert builders.build_fixture() == 1
      with mock.patch("app.builders.build_fixture"):
          pass
  ```

- **Classes**: a class with no reference outside the tests is reported under the same condition.

  ```python report file=app/records.py
  class Record:
      pass
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_records.py
  from app.records import Record


  def test_record() -> None:
      assert Record()
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Names the run uses outside the tests**: a single use from application code keeps the name.

  ```python ok file=app/shared.py
  def shared() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.shared import shared


  def run() -> int:
      return shared()
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_shared.py
  from app.shared import shared


  def test_shared() -> None:
      assert shared() == 1
  ```

- **Modules the run loads as a value**: a module that production code binds and passes on, as `CODEC = fast` does, may
  have each of its functions called through that value, so none of its names is reported.

  ```python ok file=app/fast.py
  def decode(text: str) -> str:
      return text
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app import fast

  CODEC = fast
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_fast.py
  from app import fast


  def test_decode() -> None:
      assert fast.decode("1") == "1"
  ```

  The same holds for a module reached as `app.fast` in `CODEC = app.fast`. A function body's import counts only when
  that function loads the name it binds as a value, as `fast` in `return fast` does, so a function that only calls
  `fast.decode()` leaves the module's other functions reported.

  ```python ok file=app/fast.py
  def decode(text: str) -> str:
      return text
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  import app.fast

  CODEC = app.fast
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_fast.py
  from app import fast


  def test_decode() -> None:
      assert fast.decode("1") == "1"
  ```

  A function that imports the module and loads its name as a value counts the same way:

  ```python ok file=app/fast.py
  def decode(text: str) -> str:
      return text
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  def codec():
      from app import fast

      return fast
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_fast.py
  from app import fast


  def test_decode() -> None:
      assert fast.decode("1") == "1"
  ```

  An import in a class body binds a class attribute, which other code reads as `Service.codec` without naming the
  module, so it counts whatever the name is used for:

  ```python ok file=app/fast.py
  def decode(text: str) -> str:
      return text
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  class Service:
      from app import fast as codec


  def run(text: str) -> str:
      return Service.codec.decode(text)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_fast.py
  from app import fast


  def test_decode() -> None:
      assert fast.decode("1") == "1"
  ```

- **A library's public API**: a name a public module offers, or that a user of the library may import, is public even
  when the tests are its only importers. The docstring rules decide what is public, so this rule reuses that decision.

  ```toml config
  [build-system]
  requires = ["setuptools"]

  [project]
  name = "mylib"
  ```

  ```python ok file=mylib/api.py
  def build_fixture() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_api.py
  from mylib.api import build_fixture


  def test_build() -> None:
      assert build_fixture() == 1
  ```

- **Names with no reference at all**: dead code is a different concern, so a function nothing calls is not reported
  here.

  ```python ok
  def unused() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

- **Entry points** named in `pyproject.toml`, which the program runs without any import.

  ```toml config
  [project]
  name = "tool"

  [project.scripts]
  tool = "app.cli:main"
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/cli.py
  def main() -> None:
      pass
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_cli.py
  from app.cli import main


  def test_main() -> None:
      main()
  ```

- **Modules a `.pth` file loads at startup**: the interpreter runs the `import` lines of a `.pth` file in a source
  directory when it starts, so a name those lines read is kept. A path line runs nothing.

  ```python ok file=app/hook.py
  def _run() -> None:
      print("hook")
  ```

  ```python context file=app.pth
  # fmt: off
  import app.hook; app.hook._run()
  # fmt: on
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_hook.py
  from app.hook import _run


  def test_run() -> None:
      _run()
  ```

- **Decorated definitions**: a decorator may register the definition with something outside the run, such as a plugin
  list or a framework, so any decorated function or class is kept.

  ```python ok file=app/registry.py
  from functools import cache


  @cache
  def build_fixture() -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_registry.py
  from app.registry import build_fixture


  def test_build() -> None:
      assert build_fixture() == 1
  ```

- **Dunder names** such as `__getattr__`, which the interpreter reads without an import.

  ```python ok file=app/lazy.py
  def __getattr__(name: str) -> int:
      return 1
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_lazy.py
  from app.lazy import __getattr__


  def test_lazy() -> None:
      assert __getattr__("x") == 1
  ```

- **Names the module uses itself**: a call from elsewhere in the module, or a name listed in `__all__`, keeps the
  definition, since the module needs it whatever the tests do. A recursive call inside the definition does not count.

  ```python ok file=app/tools.py
  def normalize(text: str) -> str:
      return text.strip()


  def clean(text: str) -> str:
      return normalize(text)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_tools.py
  from app.tools import normalize


  def test_normalize() -> None:
      assert normalize(" a ") == "a"
  ```

- **Test modules**: a module that is itself a test module is not checked.

  ```python ok file=tests/helpers.py
  def make_user() -> str:
      return "alice"
  ```

The rule has no fix, because moving code into the tests changes the layout of the project, which the author decides.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet.

name: unused-definition
summary: Functions, classes, methods and class attributes nothing in the run uses
explanation: Flags functions, classes, methods and class attributes that nothing in the run uses, so the program never reaches them. ## Why is this bad? Code nothing calls still has to be read, kept compiling and updated when its neighbors change. Readers spend time working out whether it matters, and the test suite rarely covers it, so it drifts. Removing it keeps the module to what the program does. ## Example ```python report def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" print("ready") ``` Use instead: ```python ok print("ready") ``` ## What it does A name counts as used when the run imports it, reads it through a module, names it in a dotted string, a doctest uses it, refers to it elsewhere in its own module, or spells it in a string of its module, as a string annotation does. A read of `obj.name` anywhere in the run counts as a use of every function, class, method and class attribute named `name`, since the object may be a module the run loads under a computed name. The project's documentation counts too: a definition a Sphinx page names is used. ### Active on - **Module-level functions and classes** that no reference in the run reaches. ```python report def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" print("ready") ``` ```python report class Record: pass print("ready") ``` - **Methods** of a module-level class without bases or decorators, when no `obj.name` read of the method name exists in the run. ```python report class Client: def send(self, data: str) -> None: print(data) print(Client()) ``` - **Class attributes**: plain `NAME = value` assignments in the same kind of class, which nothing reads. ```python report class Client: RETRIES = 3 def send(self) -> None: print("sent") print(Client().send()) ``` ### Exceptions - **Names used elsewhere in the run**: a function imported by another module, or called from the module itself, is used. ```python ok file=app/format.py def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` ```python context file=app/main.py from app.format import format_name print(format_name("Ada", "Lovelace")) ``` - **Names read by a dotted string**: a `"pkg.module.name"` string, such as the target of `mock.patch`, counts as a read. ```python ok file=app/format.py def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` ```python context file=tests/test_format.py from unittest import mock def test_format() -> None: with mock.patch("app.format.format_name"): pass ``` - **Names listed in `__all__`**: the module exports them, so the run may use them from outside. - **Names doctests use**: a `>>>` example in a docstring reads each name it uses, whether it imports the name or not, since a doctest runs in the globals of the module that defines the name, so the example may sit in that module. ```python ok file=app/markup.py class _Escaped: """Escapes text. >>> from app.markup import _Escaped >>> _Escaped() # doctest: +SKIP """ ``` ```python ok __all__ = ["format_name"] def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` - **Names a class body or a string uses**: a class attribute such as `x = property(_get_x)` reads the method, and a string annotation reads the class it names. ```python ok from typing import cast class _Entry: pass class Point: def _get_x(self) -> int: return 1 x = property(_get_x) print(Point().x, cast("list[_Entry]", [])) ``` - **Private protocols and TypedDicts Ruff reports**: when the project's Ruff configuration selects [PYI046](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-private-protocol/) or [PYI049](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-private-typed-dict/), Ruff reports a private `Protocol` or `TypedDict` class that nothing in its file reads, so this rule leaves it to Ruff. ```toml config [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["PYI046", "PYI049"] ``` ```python ok from typing import Protocol, TypedDict class _Runner(Protocol): def run(self) -> None: ... class _Row(TypedDict): a: int print("ready") ``` - **Names read off an object**: an `obj.name` read may reach a module, so it keeps every definition named `name`. ```python ok file=app/sysroot.py def _default_sysroot() -> str: return "/" ``` ```python context file=app/main.py import importlib module = importlib.import_module("app.sysroot") print(module._default_sysroot()) ``` - **Names the documentation gives**: a `.rst` or `.md` file under the project names a definition with a Sphinx role such as `:func:`, an autodoc directive such as `.. autofunction::`, or the `:module:` and `:func:` options of a sphinx-argparse or sphinx-argparse-cli directive. An `.. automodule::` with `:members:` documents the members Sphinx renders: the names its module's `__all__` lists, or else its public names, without the ones `:exclude-members:` names, and with the private and special names when `:private-members:` or `:special-members:` is set. For a package the module is its `__init__.py`. Its classes' members are documented too, and so is every member of an `.. autoclass::` with `:members:`. Names match by their dotted ending, so a page under `.. currentmodule::`, or one whose `conf.py` puts another directory on `sys.path`, still matches. The files are read from the directory of each `pyproject.toml`, outside hidden directories and the paths Ruff excludes. ```toml config [project] name = "app" ``` ```python ok file=app/cli.py from argparse import ArgumentParser def build_parser() -> ArgumentParser: return ArgumentParser(prog="app") ``` ```rst context file=docs/cli.rst .. sphinx_argparse_cli:: :module: app.cli :func: build_parser ``` ```toml config [project] name = "app" ``` ```python ok file=app/format.py def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` ```markdown context file=docs/api.md Call {py:func}`~app.format.format_name` to join the parts. ``` - **A library's public API**: a name a public module offers may be used by code outside the run. ```toml config [build-system] requires = ["setuptools"] [project] name = "mylib" ``` ```python ok file=mylib/api.py def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` - **Decorated definitions**: a decorator may register the definition with something outside the run, such as a plugin list or a framework. ```python ok from functools import cache @cache def format_name(first: str, last: str) -> str: return f"{first} {last}" ``` - **Framework hooks**: `setup` and `teardown` functions, and `pytest_*` hooks, are called by Sphinx or pytest by name, and so are the hooks of the build backend that `build-backend` names in `[build-system]`, which a build frontend calls. With `pdm.backend`, functions in the local `pdm_build.py` file or its `[tool.pdm.build] custom-hook` replacement are build hooks too. ```python ok file=docs/conf.py def setup(app: object) -> None: print(app) ``` - **hatchling custom hooks**: hatchling calls the class that subclasses `BuildHookInterface` or `MetadataHookInterface` in the file a custom hook loads. A hook is declared in `[tool.hatch.build.hooks.custom]`, `[tool.hatch.build.targets..hooks.custom]` or `[tool.hatch.metadata.hooks.custom]`, or in the same table of a `hatch.toml` next to `pyproject.toml`, which overrides the keys it sets. The file is the `path` the table gives, `hatch_build.py` in the project's directory by default, after `..` is collapsed. The class may subclass a class of the run that subclasses the interface, and the other classes of the file are still judged. A hook given as a `get_build_hook()` function instead of a class is out of scope and is not read. ```toml config [tool.hatch] build.hooks.custom = {} ``` ```python ok file=hatch_build.py from hatchling.builders.hooks.plugin.interface import BuildHookInterface class _CustomBuildHook(BuildHookInterface): def initialize(self, version: str, build_data: dict[str, object]) -> None: print(version, build_data) ``` - **Coverage plugins**: coverage loads each module that `[tool.coverage.run] plugins` in `pyproject.toml` lists by its dotted name and calls its `coverage_init`, so no import reaches the function. The module is found in the project's directory or in a directory the `pythonpath` of pytest or the `extra-paths` of ty adds to the project's import path. Only that function is read; the other definitions of the module are judged as usual. ```toml config [tool.coverage.run] plugins = ["tasks.coverage_pragmas"] ``` ```python ok file=tasks/coverage_pragmas.py def coverage_init(reg: object, options: dict[str, str]) -> None: pass ``` - **Tool references in `pyproject.toml`**: setuptools dynamic attributes and command classes, mypy and Pylint plugin functions, Poetry plugin entry points, and pytest plugins loaded through `addopts` count as used. For a bare pytest plugin module, its public hooks count as used by the host. - **Dunder and sunder names** such as `__repr__`, which the interpreter calls without a name in the source, and `_repr_html_` or `_missing_`, which Jupyter and `enum` call by name. ```python ok class Record: def __repr__(self) -> str: return "Record" def _repr_html_(self) -> str: return "Record" print(Record()) ``` - **Methods and attributes of classes with bases**: a base class may call the method, or a framework may. Classes with a decorator are left alone for the same reason. ```python ok class Base: pass class Client(Base): def send(self, data: str) -> None: print(data) print(Client()) ``` - **Test modules**: a test module's helpers belong to the tests, and pytest may call them by name. ```python ok file=tests/test_helpers.py def make_user() -> str: return "alice" ``` - **Computed attribute reads**: a read under a name computed at run time, such as `getattr(obj, name)`, `vars(obj)` or `dir(obj)`, may reach any name of the module it sits in, and any public name of the run. A private name is therefore kept only when its own file makes such a read. A name built on a literal start, as `getattr(self, "_handle_" + kind)` or `getattr(self, f"_handle_{kind}")` builds for a dispatch table, reaches only the names with that start, wherever they are defined; a start of underscores alone picks out no family, so it counts as any name. ```python ok class Client: def send(self) -> None: print("sent") def call(client: Client, name: str) -> object: return getattr(client, name) print(call(Client(), "send")) ``` ```python ok file=app/handlers.py class Handlers: def _handle_text(self) -> None: print("text") print(Handlers()) ``` ```python context file=app/dispatch.py def dispatch(handlers: object, kind: str) -> object: return getattr(handlers, "_handle_" + kind) ``` A name outside the family is still judged, in the file of the read as well: ```python report class Handlers: def _handle_text(self) -> None: print("text") def _render(self) -> None: print("render") def dispatch(handlers: Handlers, kind: str) -> object: return getattr(handlers, f"_handle_{kind}") print(dispatch(Handlers(), "text")) ``` ### Fix The rule has no fix. Deleting a definition can strand the imports it used, and it changes the program when something outside the run reads the name in a way simplint cannot see, such as a plugin loaded by name. The author decides what to remove. ## Other tools - **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rules [PYI046](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-private-protocol/) and [PYI049](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-private-typed-dict/), which report a private `Protocol` or `TypedDict` unused in its own file and which this rule leaves to them; unused definitions across the project are open issue [#872](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/872). - [vulture](https://github.com/jendrikseipp/vulture) reports unused functions, classes, methods and attributes across the files it is given, with a confidence score and no fix. - [deadcode](https://github.com/albertas/deadcode) reports the same definitions as [DC02](https://github.com/albertas/deadcode) to DC04, and its `--fix` option deletes them. This rule offers no fix, since a deletion can strand the imports the definition used.

name: test-only-parameter
summary: Parameters only test calls pass, which production calls leave at their default
explanation:
Flags a parameter with a default that only test calls pass, while production calls leave it at the default.

## Why is this bad?

A parameter that only tests set is a seam for the test suite in production code. Callers see an option the program never
uses, and the variation it offers lives where no reader expects it. Keeping the variation in the tests, through a helper
or a fixture, leaves the production signature to what the program does.

## Example

```python context file=app/service.py
from app.mail import send


def notify(address: str) -> None:
    send(address)
```

```python report file=app/mail.py
def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
    print(address, urgent)
```

```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
from app.mail import send


def test_send() -> None:
    send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
```

Use instead:

```python ok file=app/mail.py
def send(address: str) -> None:
    print(address, False)
```

```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
from app.mail import send


def test_send() -> None:
    send("a@b.c")
```

## What it does

For each module-level function, the rule compares the calls that production code makes with the calls tests make. A
production call that passes an argument by position or by keyword counts for that parameter, and so does one that
unpacks `**kwargs`, which may pass any keyword.

### Active on

- **Defaulted parameters that no production call passes**, when at least one test call passes them and production code
  calls the function at least once. A required parameter is always passed, so it is never reported.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str) -> None:
      send(address)
  ```

  ```python report file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

- **Keyword-only parameters**, which a call passes only by keyword.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str) -> None:
      send(address)
  ```

  ```python report file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, *, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Parameters production code passes**: a single production call that passes the parameter keeps it.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str) -> None:
      send(address, urgent=True)
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

- **Modules a program runs**: a module with an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block runs as production code even when a
  test imports it, so its calls count as production calls.

  ```python context file=app/notify.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str) -> None:
      send(address)
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def escalate(address: str) -> None:
      send(address, urgent=True)


  if __name__ == "__main__":
      escalate("a@b.c")
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_service.py
  from app.service import escalate


  def test_escalate() -> None:
      escalate("a@b.c")
  ```

  A module that production code star-imports runs as production code too, so its calls count the same way:

  ```python context file=app/notify.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str) -> None:
      send(address)
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def escalate(address: str) -> None:
      send(address, urgent=True)
  ```

  ```python context file=app/__main__.py
  from app.service import *


  escalate("a@b.c")
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_service.py
  from app.service import escalate


  def test_escalate() -> None:
      escalate("a@b.c")
  ```

- **Functions with no production call**: a function only tests call is test support, which `test-only-code` reports
  instead.

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

- **Functions used other than as a call**: passed as a value, or named by a dotted string or an entry point, where the
  calls that reach them are not all visible.

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)


  HANDLERS = [send]
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

- **Decorated functions**: a decorator may register or wrap the function, so its calls may not be the ones written.

  ```python ok
  from functools import cache


  @cache
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)


  send("a@b.c")
  ```

- **Public functions of a library**: code outside the project may call them without the argument.

  ```toml config
  [build-system]
  requires = ["setuptools"]

  [project]
  name = "mylib"
  ```

  ```python ok file=mylib/api.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_api.py
  from mylib.api import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

- **A program's entry**: a call from an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block or a `__main__.py` runs the module as a
  program, whose arguments come from the command line, so `main(argv=None)` leaves `argv` out on purpose.

  ```python ok file=app/cli.py
  def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
      return len(argv or [])


  if __name__ == "__main__":
      main()
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_cli.py
  from app.cli import main


  def test_main() -> None:
      assert main(["a"]) == 1
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/run.py
  def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
      return len(argv or [])
  ```

  ```python context file=app/__main__.py
  from app.run import main

  main()
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_run.py
  from app.run import main


  def test_main() -> None:
      assert main(["a"]) == 1
  ```

- **Modules only tests import**: a helper module outside the test directories, such as `testing/fixtures.py`, that only
  test modules import, directly or through other such modules, serves the tests, so its calls are test code.

  ```python ok file=testing/fixtures.py
  def make_config(rev: str = "main") -> str:
      return rev


  def default_config() -> str:
      return make_config()
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_config.py
  from testing.fixtures import default_config, make_config


  def test_config() -> None:
      assert make_config(rev="v1") != default_config()
  ```

- **Calls that unpack `*args` or `**kwargs`**: the unpacked values may pass the parameter.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.mail import send


  def notify(address: str, options: dict[str, bool]) -> None:
      send(address, **options)
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/mail.py
  def send(address: str, urgent: bool = False) -> None:
      print(address, urgent)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_mail.py
  from app.mail import send


  def test_send() -> None:
      send("a@b.c", urgent=True)
  ```

### Fix

The rule has no fix. Removing the parameter changes the signature every caller sees, and the tests that pass it would
need the variation moved elsewhere first. The author decides where the variation belongs.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet.

name: unused-return-value
summary: Return values no production call reads
explanation:
Flags a function whose return value no production call reads: its callers drop the value, or only tests read it.

## Why is this bad?

A `return` that nothing uses is a promise the function keeps for nobody. Readers take the value to matter, look for the
caller that consumes it, and find none. Returning nothing says what the function does, and it lets the function stop
building a value that is thrown away.

## Example

```python context file=app/service.py
from app.store import save_order


def place_order(order: str) -> None:
    save_order(order)
```

```python report file=app/store.py
def save_order(order: str) -> str:
    print("saved", order)
    return order
```

Use instead:

```python ok file=app/store.py
def save_order(order: str) -> None:
    print("saved", order)
```

## What it does

For each function that returns a value, the rule checks every call the run makes. A call on a line of its own drops the
value, as `save_order(order)` does, and a call inside an expression reads it. The function is reported when production
code calls it and no production call reads the value, whether or not tests read it.

### Active on

- **Module-level functions** whose calls in production code all drop the value.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.store import save_order


  def place_order(order: str) -> None:
      save_order(order)
  ```

  ```python report file=app/store.py
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      print("saved", order)
      return order
  ```

- **Functions whose value only tests read**: a test that reads the value does not count as a production use.

  ```python report file=app/store.py
  def load_total(order: str) -> int:
      return len(order)
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.store import load_total


  def place_order(order: str) -> None:
      load_total(order)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_store.py
  from app.store import load_total


  def test_total() -> None:
      assert load_total("abc") == 3
  ```

- **Methods called through `self`**: a method of a module-level class without bases, when every read of its name in the
  run is a `self.name(...)` call inside the class.

  ```python report
  class Writer:
      def write(self, data: str) -> int:
          return len(data)

      def commit(self, data: str) -> None:
          self.write(data)
  ```

### Exceptions

- **Functions whose value a production call reads**: one reading call keeps the function.

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.store import save_order


  def place_order(order: str) -> int:
      return len(save_order(order))
  ```

  ```python ok file=app/store.py
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      print("saved", order)
      return order
  ```

- **Functions with no return value, or that return only `self`**: a function that returns nothing, or only `None`, has
  no value to read, and a method that returns `self` lets callers chain calls, a style of its interface.

  ```python ok
  class Query:
      def where(self, clause: str) -> "Query":
          print(clause)
          return self

      def run(self) -> None:
          self.where("a = 1")


  Query().run()
  ```

  ```python ok
  def save_order(order: str) -> None:
      print("saved", order)


  save_order("a")
  ```

- **Functions only tests call**: a function production code never calls is test support, which `test-only-code` reports.

  ```python ok file=app/store.py
  def load_total(order: str) -> int:
      return len(order)
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_store.py
  from app.store import load_total


  def test_total() -> None:
      assert load_total("abc") == 3
  ```

- **Functions with no call**: nothing calls them, so the rule has no call to judge. `unused-definition` reports them.

  ```python ok
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      return order
  ```

- **Functions used other than as a call**: passed as a value, or named by a dotted string or an entry point, where the
  calls that reach them are not all visible.

  ```python ok file=app/store.py
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      return order


  HANDLERS = [save_order]
  ```

  ```python context file=app/service.py
  from app.store import save_order


  def place_order(order: str) -> None:
      save_order(order)
  ```

- **A program's entry**: a call from an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block or a `__main__.py` hands the value to the
  command line, which may use it as the exit status.

  ```python ok
  def main() -> int:
      return 0


  if __name__ == "__main__":
      main()
  ```

- **Modules only tests import**: a helper module outside the test directories that only test modules import, directly or
  through other such modules, serves the tests, so its calls are test code.

  ```python ok file=testing/util.py
  def git_commit(message: str) -> str:
      return message


  def commit_all() -> None:
      git_commit("all")
  ```

  ```python context file=tests/test_git.py
  from testing.util import commit_all, git_commit


  def test_commit() -> None:
      commit_all()
      assert git_commit("a") == "a"
  ```

- **Decorated functions**: a decorator may wrap the function or use its value, so its calls may not be the ones written.

  ```python ok
  from functools import cache


  @cache
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      return order


  save_order("a")
  ```

- **Dunder methods**: Python calls them itself, not by name.

  ```python ok
  class Order:
      def __str__(self) -> str:
          return "order"


  print(Order())
  ```

- **Public API**: the public functions and methods of a library, and the names `__all__` lists, may be called by code
  outside the run.

  ```toml config
  [build-system]
  requires = ["setuptools"]

  [project]
  name = "mylib"
  ```

  ```python ok file=mylib/api.py
  def save_order(order: str) -> str:
      return order
  ```

  ```python context file=mylib/service.py
  from mylib.api import save_order


  def place_order(order: str) -> None:
      save_order(order)
  ```

- **Methods of classes with bases, or whose name is read elsewhere**: a subclass may override the method, and a read of
  the name through another object hides which method it reaches.

  ```python ok
  class Base:
      pass


  class Writer(Base):
      def write(self, data: str) -> int:
          return len(data)

      def commit(self, data: str) -> None:
          self.write(data)


  Writer().commit("a")
  ```

### Fix

The rule has no fix. Dropping the `return` changes the signature that tests and outside callers of a library may read,
and the value may be the only thing a caller keeps. The author decides whether the caller or the function should change.

## Other tools

- **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** not requested yet.

name: walrus-candidate
summary: An assignment the next `if` test could absorb with `:=`
explanation:
Flags an assignment to a name that only feeds the `if` statement right after it. Inlining the value, or binding it in the test with `:=`, keeps the value next to the check that uses it. ## Why is this bad? A name that exists only to feed the next test splits one decision over two statements. It also stays in scope after it stops mattering. Inlining the value, or binding it in the test with an [assignment expression](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#assignment-expressions) (`:=`, from [PEP 572](https://peps.python.org/pep-0572/)), keeps the value next to the check that uses it. ## Example ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = re.match(r"\w+", text) if found: return found.group(0) stripped = text.strip() if not stripped: return "" return text ``` Use instead: ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: if found := re.match(r"\w+", text): return found.group(0) if not text.strip(): return "" return text ``` ## Configuration - [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python); see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version) ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py37" ``` ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length) and [`indent-width`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#indent-width), which give the width an `if` header must fit; see [Settings shared with Ruff](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#settings-shared-with-ruff) ```toml config [tool.ruff] line-length = 40 ``` ```python ok def check(text: str) -> bool: size = len(text) + len(text) + len(text) + len(text) if size > 1000000: return True return False ``` ## What it does ### Active on An assignment to a single name is reported when it is directly followed by an `if` statement whose test starts with that name, and nothing else reads the name: not after the `if` statement, and not before the assignment either, such as a closure or an earlier statement of the same loop. The search covers the enclosing function, or the whole file at module level. The test starts with the name when the name is: - **The whole test**, as in `if found:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str) -> str: if found := text.strip(): return found return "" ``` - **The operand of `not`**, as in `if not found:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if not found: return "" return text ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str) -> str: if not text.strip(): return "" return text ``` - **The left side of a comparison**, as in `if found > 3:`. ```python report def long_enough(text: str) -> bool: size = len(text) if size > 3: return True return False ``` ```python fixed def long_enough(text: str) -> bool: if len(text) > 3: return True return False ``` - **The first operand of `and` or `or`**, as in `if found and ready:`. ```python report def first_word(text: str, ready: bool) -> str: found = text.strip() if found and ready: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def first_word(text: str, ready: bool) -> str: if (found := text.strip()) and ready: return found return "" ``` In each case the value can take the name's place at the start of the test without changing what runs first. ### Exceptions - **Target versions older than 3.8**: Python 3.8 introduced `:=`. ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py37" ``` ```python ok def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - **Modules with a version gate**, as [missing-final](SMP601.html) describes: the module exists to run on older interpreters and report them. ```python ok import sys if sys.version_info < (3, 8): raise SystemExit("Python 3.8 or newer is required") def first_word(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` - **Assignments in a class body**, including inside an `if`, `for` or `try` block of the class, unless a function sits between: such an assignment defines a class attribute, which `Class.name` reads without a name reference. ```python ok class Config: found = len("text") if found: LIMIT = found ``` - **Values that are a lambda, `yield`, `yield from`, an `:=` expression or a tuple without parentheses**: these are not reported. ```python ok def run(items: list[str]) -> list[str]: found = lambda: items if found: return found() return items ``` - **Values that mention the name itself**: these are not reported. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() or found if found: return found return text ``` - **Assignments that share a line with other code**: the fix deletes the assignment's whole line. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() other = 1 if found: return found return str(other) ``` - **Assignments with a comment on their line, or between them and the `if`**: deleting the assignment would lose the comment. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() # the stripped text if found: return found return text ``` - **`TYPE_CHECKING`**: type checkers recognize the guard by that name whatever its value, so the name must stay. ```python ok TYPE_CHECKING = False if TYPE_CHECKING: import os ``` - **Module-level names that another module in the run imports or patches by name, or that `__all__` lists, and every module-level name when `__all__` is computed**: the other module would lose the binding. ```python ok file=settings.py found = len("text") if found: print(found) ``` ```python context file=main.py from settings import found ``` - **Names the function declares [`global`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-global-statement) or [`nonlocal`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-nonlocal-statement)**: code in the outer scope reads the binding too. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: global found found = text.strip() if found: return found return text ``` - **A name in a function that also mentions `locals`, `vars`, `eval` or `exec`, or a module-level name in a file that mentions one of them or `globals`**: those calls find names by their text, so removing the binding would hide it from them. At module level the search covers the whole file, functions included. ```python ok def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return str(locals()) return "" ``` ```python ok found = len("text") if found: print(found) print(globals()) ``` - **An `if` whose header, with the value folded in, would not fit [`line-length`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#line-length) on one line at its block's indentation**: `ruff format` would split it over several lines, which reads worse than the two statements. The header is measured joined on one line without parentheses around the test, which the formatter drops, so how the code is laid out now does not matter. A header with a comment or a string over several lines never fits. ```python ok def run(text: str, flag: bool) -> str: found = text.strip() if flag and found and text.startswith("a") and text.endswith("b") and text.isalpha() and text.isascii(): return found return text ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD assign["name = value"] --> test{"next if test
starts with name?"} test -->|no| skip["not reported"] test -->|yes| read{"name read
anywhere else?"} read -->|yes| skip read -->|no| skipped{"skipped case, or
header too long?"} skipped -->|yes| skip skipped -->|no| again{"name used again
in the if?"} again -->|yes| walrus["fix: name := value
in the test"] again -->|no| inline["fix: inline the value"] classDef blue fill:#9cc0e3,stroke:#1f4f7d,color:#062d59 classDef yellow fill:#f2d27a,stroke:#6b5410,color:#062d59 classDef green fill:#93cfa9,stroke:#1d5e3a,color:#0b2e1a classDef teal fill:#8ccbc3,stroke:#145c55,color:#072b28 classDef orange fill:#f0b48c,stroke:#8a3d12,color:#3d1606 class assign blue class test,read,skipped,again yellow class skip green class walrus,inline teal ``` ### Fix The fix is safe. It deletes the assignment, then: - when the name appears nowhere else in the `if` statement, including the rest of the test, the body and any `elif` or `else` branch, it inlines the value and adds parentheses where precedence requires them; ```python report def run(text: str) -> bool: found = text.strip() + "!" if found: return True return False ``` ```python fixed def run(text: str) -> bool: if text.strip() + "!": return True return False ``` - otherwise it writes `name := value` in the test, in parentheses unless the name is the whole test. ```python report def run(text: str) -> str: found = text.strip() if found: return found return "" ``` ```python fixed def run(text: str) -> str: if found := text.strip(): return found return "" ``` When the assignment and the `if` it leads to are the only statements of an `if` whose header holds a comment, and that `if` has no `else` or `elif` branch, Ruff would merge the two `if` statements only past the comment. The fix would leave that work behind, so the finding is reported without a fix. ```python report def run(text: str, flag: bool) -> str: if flag: # keep size = len(text) if size > 3: return text return "" ``` The search for other reads looks only at names in code. It misses importers outside the run and references held in strings, such as an `__all__` entry. ## Other tools - **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** open issues [#970](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/970), [#11060](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11060) and [#10108](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/10108). - [pylint](https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint) reports the same assignment and `if` pairs as [consider-using-assignment-expr](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/messages/refactor/consider-using-assignment-expr.html), for targets that allow `:=`, with no fix.

name: string-concatenation
summary: `+` between strings
explanation:
Flags `+` chains that join a string literal or f-string with other values. An f-string shows the final text in one piece, where a `+` chain scatters it across quotes and operators. ## Why is this bad? A chain of `+` scatters the text across quotes and operators, and every non-string operand needs an explicit `str()`. An f-string ([PEP 498](https://peps.python.org/pep-0498/)) shows the final text in one piece. ## Example ```python report message = "Hello, " + name + "!" ``` Use instead: ```python ok message = f"Hello, {name}!" ``` ## Configuration - [`target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#target-version) and [`per-file-target-version`](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/settings/#per-file-target-version), falling back to [`project.requires-python`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#requires-python); see [Python version](https://simplint.readthedocs.io/en/latest/configuration/project.html#python-version) ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311" ``` ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.strip('"') + "!" ``` ## What it does ### Active on - **`+` chains that join a string literal or [f-string](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#f-strings) with other values**, such as `"Hello, " + name + "!"`: the whole chain is reported once. **Unsafe fix:** always, and offered only when the code shows every operand is a `str`. `+` raises [`TypeError`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#TypeError) for a non-string operand and honors a custom [`__add__`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__add__) or `__radd__`, such as `markupsafe.Markup` escaping the other operand, while an f-string formats any value. ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name + "!" ``` ```python fixed def greet(name: str) -> str: return f"Hello, {name}!" ``` ### Exceptions - **Chains that contain a bytes literal**: Python has no bytes f-string to write them as. ```python ok def header(name: bytes) -> bytes: return b"Name: " + name ``` - **The message of a logging call**, such as `logger.info("Hello, " + name)`: Ruff's [logging-string-concat](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/logging-string-concat/) reports it while the project's Ruff configuration selects it, so this rule leaves it to Ruff. ```toml config [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["G003"] ``` ```python ok import logging logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) def greet(name: str) -> None: logger.info("Hello, " + name) ``` - **Two literals joined by `+` across lines**, such as `("Hello, "` followed by `+ "world")`: Ruff's [explicit-string-concatenation](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/explicit-string-concatenation/) reports it while the project's Ruff configuration selects it and `allow-multiline` is on, so this rule leaves it to Ruff. A longer chain that starts with such a pair is left to Ruff as well, since both would report the same spot. ```toml config [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["ISC003"] ``` ```python ok # fmt: off title = ( "Hello, " + "world" ) # fmt: on ``` - **Chains with an operand that is an instance of a class**, such as `Markup("")` for a `Markup` class that overrides `__add__` or one `markupsafe` provides: `+` runs that method, which an f-string would not, so the chain is left alone. The instance may come from a call, a variable holding one, a parameter annotated with the class, a method of such an instance, or a function of the module annotated to return it. A class the run defines is recognized under any name, and a name imported from outside the run counts as a class when its name is CapWords, as PEP 8 spells classes, with leading underscores ignored, so `_Private` counts too. ```python ok class Markup(str): def __add__(self, other: str) -> "Markup": return Markup(str.__add__(self, other.replace("<", "<"))) SAFE = Markup("") + "" ``` ```python ok from markupsafe import Markup SAFE = Markup("") + "" ``` - **Chains with a string in a non-literal operand that holds a backslash, on a target before Python 3.12**, such as `"a" + name.strip("\n")`: a replacement field of an f-string cannot hold a backslash inside a string before [PEP 701](https://peps.python.org/pep-0701/#considerations-of-quote-reuse), so no f-string holds the chain for that target and this rule does not report it. From Python 3.12 on the chain is reported as before. ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311" ``` ```python ok def trim(name: str) -> str: return "a" + name.strip("\n") ``` ### Deciding on a fix ```mermaid flowchart TD chain["+ chain with a string"] --> bytes{"holds a
bytes literal?"} bytes -->|yes| skip["not reported"] bytes -->|no| instance{"holds an instance of a class,
or a call to an imported class?"} instance -->|yes| skip instance -->|no| target{"holds a backslash in a string
before Python 3.12?"} target -->|yes| skip target -->|no| known{"every operand
known str?"} known -->|no| none["reported, no fix"] known -->|yes| fits{"chain fits
an f-string?"} fits -->|no| none fits -->|yes| fix["reported,
unsafe fix"] classDef blue fill:#9cc0e3,stroke:#1f4f7d,color:#062d59 classDef yellow fill:#f2d27a,stroke:#6b5410,color:#062d59 classDef green fill:#93cfa9,stroke:#1d5e3a,color:#0b2e1a classDef teal fill:#8ccbc3,stroke:#145c55,color:#072b28 classDef orange fill:#f0b48c,stroke:#8a3d12,color:#3d1606 class chain blue class bytes,instance,target,known,fits yellow class skip green class none orange class fix teal ``` ### Known `str` operands An operand is known to be a `str` when it is one of these. Literals and expressions: - a string literal or f-string, `"..." % values`, or a `str` repeated by an `int`, such as `"-" * width` - an index or slice of a `str`, or an item of a list, tuple, set or mapping of them, such as `name.split(".")[0]` or `names[0]` for `names: list[str]` - a conditional between `str` values, or `a or "default"` where `a` is a `str` or `None` Builtins and the standard library: - a call to the builtin `str`, `repr`, `ascii`, `format`, `chr`, `hex`, `oct` or `bin` - a `str` method such as `join`, `format` or `upper` called on a `str`, or `decode` on `bytes` - `__name__`, `__qualname__` and `__module__` of anything, and the module's `__name__` and `__file__` - standard library values the module imports: `os.sep`, `os.linesep`, `sys.platform`, the `string` constants, `os.getcwd()`, `platform.system()`, `json.dumps(...)`, `textwrap.dedent(...)`, `os.environ[...]`, `os.environ.get(key, "default")`, `os.getenv(key, "default")`, `uuid.uuid4().hex`, `os.path.join(...)` and the other `os.path` functions given a `str`, `re.escape` given a `str`, and the `name`, `stem`, `suffix` and `as_posix()` of a `pathlib.Path` Code of the module: - a call to a function or method of the module annotated `-> str`, undecorated or with `functools.cache` - an attribute of an instance of a class of the module that annotates it `str`, or a property annotated `-> str` - on `self`, also an attribute that the class body and its methods only ever set to such values, when nothing else writes it and no subclass may override it - a name every binding of which, in the scope it resolves to, gives such a value: an assignment, a loop over such items, a `with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as path`, or an annotation `str` (also `Final[str]`, `Annotated[str, ...]`) that no binding contradicts A name that an unannotated parameter, an import, a `global` or a type parameter binds is not known, so `value + "!"` for an unannotated `value` is reported without a fix. The annotations are trusted: a parameter annotated `str` can still receive a `str` subclass with its own `__add__`. ### Fix The fix copies each non-literal operand into a placeholder as written: - A call to the builtin `str`, `repr` or `ascii` becomes the matching conversion, as Ruff's [explicit-f-string-type-conversion](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/explicit-f-string-type-conversion/) asks, so `"n=" + str(n)` becomes `f"n={n!s}"`. ```python report def label(n: int) -> str: return "n=" + str(n) ``` ```python fixed def label(n: int) -> str: return f"n={n!s}" ``` - A generator passed bare to `str`, `repr` or `ascii` gets parentheses of its own, since a replacement field takes only a yield or star expression unparenthesized. ```python report def label(values: list[int]) -> str: return "values=" + str(value for value in values) ``` ```python fixed def label(values: list[int]) -> str: return f"values={(value for value in values)!s}" ``` - A chain of plain string literals becomes one plain string. ```python report def title() -> str: return "Hello, " + "world" ``` ```python fixed def title() -> str: return "Hello, world" ``` No fix is offered when: - a literal is triple-quoted, raw or `u`-prefixed; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return """Hello, """ + name ``` - the literals use different quote characters; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return 'Say "hi", ' + name + ". It's late." ``` - a comment sits between the operands, since the f-string has no place for it; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return ( "Hello, " # the greeting + name ) ``` - a non-literal operand contains a backslash, `#`, `:`, `!`, `{` or `}`; before Python 3.12 a backslash inside a string is an exception above, and one outside a string, such as a line continuation, is reported without a fix; ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.replace(":", "") + "!" ``` - a name is bound by a [PEP 695](https://peps.python.org/pep-0695/) type parameter of the enclosing function or class, as its kind is not known; ```toml config [project] requires-python = ">=3.12" ``` ```python report s = "x" def f[s]() -> str: return "a" + s ``` - the target Python version is older than 3.12 and a non-literal operand contains the string's quote character, which f-strings allow only from 3.12 on ([PEP 701](https://peps.python.org/pep-0701/#considerations-of-quote-reuse)). ```toml config [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311" ``` ```python report def greet(name: str) -> str: return "Hello, " + name.strip('"') + "!" ``` ## Other tools - **[Ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff):** variation of released rules [G003](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/logging-string-concat/) and [ISC003](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/explicit-string-concatenation/), which report `+` in logging calls and between two literals split across lines and which this rule leaves to them; open issue [#11060](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11060) lists Sourcery's use-fstring-for-concatenation. - [Sourcery](https://sourcery.ai) rewrites the same `+` chains as an f-string through its [use-fstring-for-concatenation](https://docs.sourcery.ai/reference/refactorings/python/use-fstring-for-concatenation/) refactoring. - [wemake-python-styleguide](https://github.com/wemake-services/wemake-python-styleguide) reports explicit string concatenation as [WPS336](https://wemake-python-styleguide.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pages/usage/violations/consistency.html#wemake_python_styleguide.violations.consistency.ExplicitStringConcatViolation) and prefers `str.format`, where this rule prefers an f-string.
